news.title: Amaechi: Buhari Promised Me APC Presidential Ticket in 2022
news.text:
Chuks Okocha in Abuja

The African Democratic Congress (ADC) vice-presidential candidate, Mr Rotimi Amaechi, has blamed his defeat in the 2022 All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential primary on his decision to follow the advice of the late President Muhammadu Buhari not to campaign ahead of the contest.

Amaechi said Buhari had assured him in writing that he would announce him as his preferred candidate, prompting him to refrain from lobbying delegates and negotiating political alliances ahead of the primary.

He disclosed this during an interview on Mainland 98.3FM’s The Situation Room programme in Lagos on Friday, while reflecting on how President Bola Tinubu defeated him to clinch the APC presidential ticket in 2022.

According to Amaechi, he considered Buhari’s position credible because the former president was his boss and believed his endorsement would give him an advantage over other aspirants.

He said, “The first mistake that I made at that primary was that I listened to President Buhari. He said to me, ‘don’t campaign, don’t do anything, I will announce you as my candidate.’

“He told me that. He put it in writing. When I write my book, I’ll put it out.”

The former Minister of Transportation said his decision not to negotiate political positions with governors and other influential party members also worked against his ambition, and gave Tinubu an opportunity to build alliances ahead of the primary.

Amaechi explained that he could have secured the support of governors by promising them political appointments, including the positions of vice-president and Secretary to the Government of the Federation.

 “Now, I didn’t do deals. So, I would have promised you vice-president, promised you SGF, and then would have gone for this primary, I would have possibly won. I would have had governors on my side.

“Because I didn’t do deals, Tinubu had the chance to do deals,” he said.

Amaechi, who was also a presidential aspirant in the 2022 APC primary, further accused Tinubu of exploiting religious sentiments to secure support from delegates, particularly in the North.

He, however, said he would not deploy religion as a political tool to win elections, describing his position as a reflection of his nationalist convictions.

The ADC chieftain alleged that a delegation of Southern Yoruba Muslims had approached governors in the North-West and appealed to them to support Tinubu on religious grounds.

He also cited the position of former Kaduna State Governor Nasir El-Rufai, whom he said had supported his presidential ambition before eventually backing Tinubu.

 “El-Rufai was my supporter. El-Rufai, in a viral video, said this is done for the faith,” Amaechi said.

He argued that appealing to religious identity for political support could deepen divisions in the country, adding that he would not encourage such an approach even if it offered him an electoral advantage.

“I wouldn’t want to run that kind of federation. There are 35 million Catholics in Nigeria. I wouldn’t want to go to the Catholic Church and say, ‘please announce me. Tell them that all Catholics must go out and vote Amaechi.’

“It will cause confusion. It will cause problems in the country. That makes me a nationalist,” he said.

Amaechi questioned the perception of Tinubu as an exceptionally strategic politician, asking why he had not become president earlier if his political success was based on an extraordinary ability to manoeuvre.

Tinubu defeated Amaechi and other aspirants at the APC presidential primary held at Eagle Square, Abuja, in June 2022, polling 1,271 votes against Amaechi’s 316.

Kemi Badenoch Tackles Trump, Says US President Deserves US Midterm Defeat

 Sunday Ehigiator

British Conservative Party leader, Kemi Badenoch, has said the United States President Donald Trump deserved his defeat in the country’s midterm elections, criticising his handling of the Iran war, trade policies and treatment of allies.

 The Independent reported yesterday that Badenoch described Trump’s electoral setback as “entirely self-inflicted” and condemned what she called his “dirty” style of politics.

The Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections, flipping at least seven Senate seats and more than two dozen House districts in a major setback for Trump’s Republican Party.

Asked whether Trump deserved the defeat, Badenoch, in an interview with The Independent’s Editor-in-Chief, Geordie Greig, replied, “Yeah. He has not been acting in the way that I would consider conservative.”

She criticised Trump’s tariffs, threats towards Canada and Greenland, and disputes with US allies, saying his actions contradicted conservative principles of free markets and better trade.

 “Where is the push for free markets and better trade… rather than protectionism, America first, the squabbling with allies? That’s not what conservatives do,” she said.

Badenoch also criticised Trump’s personal attacks on journalists and political figures, saying his conduct fell below the standards expected of a statesman.

“Trump is very charming in person, but you see the way that he talks about journalists, about individuals. It doesn’t meet the standards a statesman should meet – always wanting to get dirty in terms of insults and so on,” she said.

She said she was particularly unhappy with Trump’s remarks about British Prime Minister Keir Starmer and described his treatment of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at the White House as “awful”.

On the Iran war, Badenoch said she understood Trump’s initial decision to launch the military action, which she supported because of concerns about Iran acquiring nuclear weapons, but questioned the absence of a clear strategy.

“We don’t want them getting nuclear weapons. But where’s the plan?” she asked.

She also said she would have been content if Trump had lost the 2024 presidential election to his Democratic opponent, Kamala Harris.

Asked which of the two candidates she preferred, Badenoch said, “I would say I like them both equally. Make of that what you will.”

The Conservative leader also argued that Trump had squandered the broad coalition of voters that helped him win the presidency, including Latino voters and more Black voters than any previous Republican candidate.

“What’s the first thing he does? Tariffs, and then talking about Greenland and Canada. A lot of people were wondering, ‘What are you doing?’” she said.

Badenoch’s comments came amid wider criticism of Trump’s handling of the economy and foreign policy following the Republicans’ losses in the midterms.

Badenoch is the leader of the UK Conservative Party and Leader of the Opposition. She became Conservative leader in November 2024 after defeating Robert Jenrick in the party’s leadership contest. She previously served as the UK’s Business and Trade Secretary and Minister for Women and Equalities under former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak.

Badenoch, whose birth name is Olukemi Olufunto Adegoke, was born in Wimbledon, London, in 1980 to Nigerian parents.

news.title: In 2028 race, Democrats have new stars and Republicans have succession squabbles
news.text:
WARNER ROBINS, Georgia – Candy Bautista was smiling as she helped herself to some fluffy pancakes at a brunch buffet. A 23-year-old economics graduate struggling to find a job, she voted for the first time the day before, on Nov 3, not really expecting an electoral earthquake.

“But I went to bed in a red state and woke up in a blue one,” said Bautista, an independent voter.

The sentence captured Georgia’s dramatic swing in the 2026 midterm elections; it elected a Democrat as governor for the first time in over 20 years. 

An even more stunning upset was in neighbouring South Carolina, which chose a Democrat senator for the first time in nearly 30 years. 

Jordy Stevens, a nurse in Lexington, South Carolina, had something to do with it. His vote had always gone to the Republicans by default. “It is just how I was raised in a Republican family,” he said. 

“But this year, look what I did.” 

The high cost of petrol was the chief reason the 30-year-old went against his party. “They forgot about us,” he said. “Now I know what that vote is worth, and our government knows it too.”

Voters like Bautista and Stevens have scrambled President Donald Trump’s political coalition and set the pulses racing for the 2028 presidential election. 

For a decade, Trump so dominated the political landscape that others defined themselves through their opposition to him. Now, with his party chastened and his presidency approaching its term limit, other figures are becoming visible.

There are no major declared contenders yet, but Americans could find themselves spoilt for choice in 2028. 

The Democrats, riding on newfound confidence after the diminishment of 2024, have the more expansive field. The Republicans have the more formidable task: How much of the Trump baggage should they carry into 2028 and what can be safely disposed of without offending his base.

A Fox News/NORC voter study described their predicament. Nearly four in 10 Republicans from Trump’s Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement want his successor to adopt both his policies and his leadership style, while half want only his policies. 

Even among non-MAGA Republicans, 45% want his policies continued.

Among the independent voters, though, six in 10 want a break from both Trump’s policies and his style.

That invokes the eternal nomination problem – first rally the party faithful, then hope to succeed with voters who sneer at the faithful. 

A successful post-Trump Republican candidate can have either Trump’s coalition or the independents, the largest bloc of American voters.

Vice-President J.D. Vance, 42, has begun this negotiation. “The reason we lost is the war,” he wrote on X after the midterms. It is a useful formulation for a vice-president seeking to establish that the administration’s failure in the unpopular Iran war was not entirely his own.

But Vance has publicly defended the Iran war, whatever his reservations in behind-the-scenes White House debate. He cannot simply step aside.

Ohio adds another embarrassment. In his home state, Democrat Amy Acton defeated Vivek Ramaswamy for governor; Sherrod Brown won the Senate seat held by Vance’s appointed successor Jon Husted. 

That complicates Vance’s claim to understand the industrial Midwest, despite his hillbilly roots, and speak for the “left-behind” men and women.

Still, he remains formidable, with high visibility and access to donors. 

Secretary of State and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio has been quieter since the midterm election, with his aides moving quickly to quash rumours that he is leaving the administration. He has previously said he would not challenge Vance. 

Polls do not show it yet, but the popularity of the former Cuban American senator from Florida is second to none with the more traditional Republicans. And the man who inspired countless social media memes – an astronaut, the Easter Bunny and a cardinal – has ardent admirers within the MAGA alumni as well as independents. 

The 55-year-old has both youth and name recognition. I have never heard anyone ask “Rubio, who?” the way I had seen people shrug when Trump roped in Vance as his running mate in the presidential campaign of 2024. But Rubio, in charge of foreign affairs and national security, cannot dodge the Iran war taint either.

Safest from any association with the war is Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, 48. He has taken credit for Republican victories in Florida: Byron Donalds as governor and Ashley Moody for senator prevailed in tight races. 

The man behind Florida’s bitter culture wars has described party performance in the midterms as a near “extinction-level event” and a rebuke of Trump. 

Which Floridian can excite the party remains an open question; current surveys show a DeSantis surge, but Rubio maintains the lead.

The field could widen if Vance stays vulnerable. Texas Senator Ted Cruz, 55, has left the door open for another presidential run, and former UN ambassador Nikki Haley remains among the names discussed. Tucker Carlson, the former Fox News host, while denying presidential plans, could help shape the argument over foreign intervention, whether as a commentator, organiser or political insurgent. 

A 2024-type crowded race – when at least 10 high-profile candidates ran in the primaries – is plausible. So is a familiar outcome where a divided opposition allows the candidate with the most committed minority to prevail.

But the Republicans can nurture hope. A midterm loss is like being sentenced to hard labour; it is not a death sentence. After a Democratic wipeout in the 2010 midterms, Barack Obama was re-elected convincingly two years later.

Democrats: A wealth of new political talent

The Democrats have emerged from the midterms with a version of “100 ways to win an election”. Unlike the Republicans, they do not have to wrestle with the Trump deadweight, but they do have an ideological maze of their own. 

Before the election, the New York Times/Siena survey found that nearly half want the party to move towards the centre, while around a quarter want to swing left. 

Independents also give the Democrats a hard time. Nearly three in four want Democrats to move towards the centre. It is a sign that progressive politics does not really own the day.

Almost all polls ranking Democratic Party nominees currently show Georgia’s re-elected Senator Jon Ossoff, 39, at or near the top. The breakout star of the midterm election has emerged with a convincing argument for electability: An 18-point win in a presidential battleground Trump carried in 2024. 

His direct attacks on Trump’s corruption and fitness for office became the talk of the nation.

I saw him in a roomful of Democratic volunteers, rolling up their sleeves to go door-knocking on an overcast day. He spoke like Obama, but looked like a less polished but more earnest version of the Chicago senator in 2008. 

Some critics fault him for striving hard to create a perfect image, in the way that an expert film-maker would. And given his antecedents as an investigative documentary maker for eight years, perhaps the critics are not far wrong.

In a party that has not had a national leadership since the Biden presidency, he has stirred up undeniable excitement.

But is he the runaway hot favourite?

He has said he has “zero interest” in running. But political circumstances can change, and he is certainly not short on ambition.

One survey shows him on a par with five-term New York congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, 37. The wait is on for AOC, as she is known, to announce her run. 

The progressive politician already has national recognition, with tens of millions of social media followers, and a formidable fund-raising operation. However, beyond the liberal blue states such as New York and California, Ocasio-Cortez’s popularity remains to be tested.

A version of that question – the potential for cross-sectional appeal – also looms over Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed, the first Muslim to be elected senator. Soon after his victory in a major battleground, he registered a political action committee, seen as a precursor to a presidential run.

Inevitably, the newly blue Texas also has its own claimant. James Talarico, 37, has created a dazzling national opportunity for himself by winning a red fort once considered impregnable by Democrats. Any argument for expanding the map in 2028 has to begin with him. After all, Texas offers the prize of the second-largest number of electoral votes, after California, in a presidential contest.

Add in his squeaky clean appeal and boyish charm, and the package is too good to miss. A short Senate apprenticeship need not prevent his advancement; Obama was a junior senator when he bid for the White House. 

Still, other surveys have favoured former vice-president Kamala Harris, 62, who retains nationwide recognition and the relationships with donors and voting blocs from her 2024 run. 

California’s outgoing Governor Gavin Newsom, 59, also has viability; he has tried to cultivate a profile through mocking confrontations with Trump, and fund raising. He has also said he would not run if Harris does.

But Harris must explain why a second presidential attempt would succeed after 2024. And Newsom must defend California’s expensive housing-and-living environment and homelessness record.

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, 53, is thought to have an edge because building a Democratic presidential coalition is difficult without winning states like his. His interest is clear: He released his memoirs in January and registered a federal political committee.

His challenge, as a Jewish man, includes navigating Democratic divisions over Israel, although he opposes the Iran war.

Other governors in contention include Andy Beshear, 48, the two-time governor of Kentucky, a red state, and Illinois Governor JB Pritzker, 61, who packs an anti-Trump identity and the wealth to sustain a long campaign. 

Also popular is Pete Buttigieg, 44, former president Joe Biden’s transportation secretary and Indiana mayor, with national experience and a fund-raising network.

Former envoy to Japan and Obama aide Rahm Emanuel, 66, is considering a candidacy built around moderate renewal in opposition to candidates like Ocasio-Cortez.

As the jostling continues in the two-year marathon from now to November 2028, the Republicans must decide who can inherit Trump’s voters, while the Democrats must find someone who can unite their factious party.

Millions of voters, like Bautista and Stevens, will be watching with a renewed sense of their own power after the momentous midterms.
news.author: Bhagyashree Garekar

news.title: Young voters overwhelmingly backed Democrats this midterm election. The question is whether they'll stay
news.text:
WASHINGTON -- Andy Soma, 24, doesn’t identify with either political party, and he's been skipping elections since he became old enough to vote. But this year, disappointed with the economy and President Donald Trump's war with Iran, he cast his midterm ballot for Roy Cooper, the North Carolina Democrat now headed to the Senate.

“I would describe it as the first time that I’ve truly felt the need to vote,” said Soma, who is pursuing a Ph.D. in mathematics at North Carolina State University. He said he wanted to “kind of take a stand, if you will.”

Young voters overwhelmingly turned their backs on Republicans on Tuesday, erasing the gains Trump had made in the 2024 presidential election. Voters under age 30 moved left by double digits in nearly all the major Senate races compared with two years earlier.

It was a similar story in House campaigns across the country. The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters, showed that about three-quarters of voters under 30 supported their local Democratic candidate, while about one-quarter voted for the Republican.

The support for Democrats outpaces even 2018, when Trump's Republican Party suffered midterm losses during his first term, and is a dramatic shift from 2024, when young voters were roughly split between Trump and Democrat Kamala Harris, according to AP VoteCast, a survey of more than 120,000 voters that year.

For Soma, the tipping point was Trump's broken pledge that he would keep the U.S. out of Middle East conflicts, a sentiment that student after student echoed in interviews on the university's Raleigh campus the day after the election.

Other young voters who broke for Democrats this year said their choices were motivated by personal experiences, including working multiple jobs to get by and watching artificial intelligence data center projects advance into their communities.

“I’m trying to save money and buy a house and all that, but it’s difficult right now,” said Corey Herzog, 28, an independent-turned-Democrat in the traditionally conservative town of Celina, Ohio. Herzog works at Walmart during the day and bartends at night, all while building out a small side business selling house plants.

John Della Volpe, a pollster who regularly surveys U.S. youth for the Harvard Kennedy School’s Institute of Politics, said the whiplash over the past two elections suggests that young voters aren’t a generation of Democrats or Republicans.

“They’re up for grabs,” he said. “Especially given the state of the economy and their concerns about the future.”

In 2024, Trump won over young men. This year, many sat out or backed Democrats

To win back the presidency two years ago, Trump courted young men who felt disillusioned by economic stagnation, interventionist foreign policy, and the government's focus on diversity, equity, and inclusion. He attended football games and UFC matches and appeared on podcasts with comedians who rebuffed “cancel culture."

More than half of male voters under 30 supported him in 2024, according to AP VoteCast.

But once in office, Trump started the war with Iran and rammed through tariff policies that continued to drive up inflation. He also resisted releasing documents about convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and launched an immigration crackdown that faced widespread criticism.

"This was the perfect cocktail for disaster,” said Charlie Sabgir, director of the Washington-based Young Men Research Project.

Young voters' unhappiness on every major issue in the midterm election was palpable. Voters under 30 were more likely than older age groups to say the cost of living was crucial for their vote for Congress, and to say the U.S. was wrong to take military action against Iran.

About half of young voters said they were angry about the way things were going in the U.S. today, compared with only about one-third of voters 65 and older.

The anti-Trump backlash was particularly strong among young voters

Even in a year when anti-Trump backlash was one of the major themes, young voters stood out.

Only about one-quarter of voters under 30 said Trump is a strong leader or has the mental capacity to serve effectively as president, according to The AP Voter Poll. That’s a sharp contrast with 2024, when about half of voters under 30 felt Trump was a strong leader and mentally fit. The decline was larger than in any other age group.

“This cultural coalition and cultural cache that Trump had behind him going into 2024 — they’ve clearly soured on him,” Sabgir said.

About 6 in 10 voters under 30 said one reason for their House vote was to express opposition to Trump.

A national consortium of college Republican groups put out a statement making their dissatisfaction clear, writing that young Republicans “were not given what they were promised.”

“In the wake of last night's election results, the College Republican Patriot Coalition unequivocally lays the blame for the greatest Republican defeat by Democrats since 1974 at the feet of the Trump administration and the Republican Party,” the group said in a statement.

Kidus Girma, campaigns director for the left-leaning Sunrise Movement, said that while he was knocking on doors in Michigan, he met young men who may not typically turn out in a midterm election but did this time because they were disappointed by Trump.

He recalled one person who complained that he was struggling to find a job even though Trump was insisting the economy is going great.

“It’s like this deep disillusionment with the statements the president makes versus the material impacts people are facing in their everyday lives," Girma said.

Gen Z voters get their ‘millennial optimism’ moment. But to keep them, Democrats must deliver

Sarah Stull, an 18-year-old student at the University of Texas at Austin, thought it was funny that so many of her classmates spent Halloween dressed up as “millennial optimism,” wearing skinny jeans and infinity scarves with grins on their faces to satirize the elder generation for being unabashedly hopeful.

Stull got the joke. Like others her age, she described herself as “very sarcastic, very jaded — and do sometimes expect the worst.”

But Tuesday night, sitting in a dorm room with friends watching election results stream in, that all went out the window.

“We were freaking out, all of us were crying,” said the young Democrat, who voted for James Talarico for Senate and Gina Hinojosa for governor. “I just felt this sense of community that I had never felt before.”

She posted a video of herself and friends on TikTok, literally jumping for joy outside the Texas Capitol, captioning it “millennial optimism cause Texas went blue."

Young adults like Stull — who was 7 when Trump rode down the escalator in New York’s Trump Tower in 2015 to announce his first presidential campaign — have only ever known “the Trumpification of politics,” said Katherine Haenschen, a political science and communication professor at Northeastern University. Now that era seems to be coming to a close, bringing hope for the first time to left-leaning young people.

But it’s a fragile moment.

Dakota Hall, executive director of the progressive youth political organization Alliance for Youth Action, said he thinks young voters could shift to the right again if Democrats leading Congress don’t do enough to lower the cost of living, regulate AI and address government corruption.

“Young people have a very short leash,” Hall said. “If you do not deliver, ’28 will be a rough road ahead.”

Rankin reported from Raleigh, N.C.
news.summary: Young voters voted overwhelmingly for Democrats in the midterm elections, driven by economic concerns and disillusionment with President Donald Trump’s war in Iran.
news.author: Ali Swenson, Sarah Rankin, And Amelia Thomson-Deveaux,Houston

news.title: Politico Gloats Over 2028 Presidential Race; Skips Mention of Likely Democrat Candidates
news.text:
The gloating at Politico over the 2026 midterm election results is not only fully underway but has already extended to what they see will be a likely Democrat victory in the 2028 presidential election as you can see in this Friday wishcast by Aaron Pellish, Lauren Fedor, and Lisa Kashinsky, "The midterms blew open the 2028 map. Republicans are panicking." 

However, there is something rather odd about their story. No prospective Democrat candidates are even named. Could it be that if any of them are named it would quickly deflate their balloon filled with Hopium?

Let us now join Politico in their somewhat premature celebrations of what they believe will likely happen in 2028 sans any mention of real life candidates:

Brutal red-state losses are raising alarm among Republicans about the 2028 presidential battlefield.Democrats’ midterm blowout is upending the political calculus for future presidential campaigns, more than a dozen strategists on both sides told POLITICO. Republicans are stressing the ramifications of a major tranche of once-reliably Republican Electoral College votes being in jeopardy, while Democrats are weighing how much surprise wins on red turf should reshape their electoral strategy.

Politico's GloatFest continues until they hit a brief encounter with hard, cold election reality, which can happen when you talk to geniuses who worked on Kamala's defeat:

Democrats know that recreating their historically large estimated 14-point national popular vote blowout isn’t likely in the 2028 presidential election, and that Trump’s historic unpopularity was a major factor in the midterms.“It’s not fait accompli that any of those voters that came over will stay with us, in the same way that they didn’t stay with Donald Trump after this last cycle, or they didn’t stay with Joe Biden after 2020,” said Dan Kanninen, former battleground states director for former Vice President Kamala Harris’ 2024 campaign. But the electoral map suddenly looks a lot different to strategists than it did a few days ago.

After this brief reflection, Politico returns to joyfully drooling over the 2028 presidential election. So why was NO Democrat presidential candidate mentioned (other than invoking Kamala Harris' name as a job description position for Kanninen above)? Could it be that they know that if names of the leading candidates were conjured up it would kill the joy they are now feeling.

news.title: Trump Shares Posts Questioning Midterm Election Results
news.text: President Donald Trump shared social media posts Saturday questioning the scale of Democrats’ midterm election gains, days after saying he was “absolutely willing” to accept the results of an election that cost Republicans control of Congress. Trump reposted material on Truth Social questioning Democratic vote totals nationally and in Texas, including a post describing Gina Hinojosa’s performance in the Texas governor’s race as “Looney Tunes numbers.” The activity marks a shift in tone from election night, when Trump acknowledged Republicans’ losses and said he would accept the results. Trump has not, in the posts seen by Newsweek, said that the midterm results were fraudulent or that he no longer accepts them. Newsweek has contacted the White House and the Texas Secretary of State’s office for comment. Trump Shares Post Calling Texas Midterm Numbers ‘Looney Tunes’ One of the posts shared by Trump Saturday was from Donald Ward, who argued that unusually high Democratic turnout in Texas could not be explained by weak Republican participation. Ward noted that Republican Governor Greg Abbott received roughly 100,000 more votes than in his 2022 reelection but lost to Hinojosa, who received substantially more votes than Democratic gubernatorial nominee Beto O'Rourke had four years earlier. “The problem is Gina Hinojosa gained 1.7 million votes more than Beto O’Rourke,” the post said. “Those are Looney Tunes numbers.” Ward added that if the turnout reflected genuine enthusiasm, “lines should have been around the block at every polling station.” Ward also compared Hinojosa’s total with those of Democratic presidential nominees Kamala Harris in 2024 and Joe Biden in 2020. The post called the numbers “not normal midterms numbers.” Trump shared an image of the post on Truth Social on Saturday morning. Minutes later, Trump shared another post, this one from Kevin Bass, featuring a chart comparing the nationwide House popular vote in 2022 with projected totals for 2026. “Republican votes stayed the same. Democrats materialized 20 million new votes,” the post said. The accompanying chart listed 54.2 million Republican and 51.3 million Democratic House votes in 2022, compared with projected 2026 totals of 55.6 million Republican and 70.4 million Democratic votes. The graphic itself noted that the 2026 numbers were projections based on 85 percent of the expected vote being counted and estimated remaining ballots at the then-current rates. Trump shared the material on Truth Social Saturday morning. Neither post provided evidence that the reported results were inaccurate or the product of fraud. Trump also shared a separate graphic highlighting the longstanding historical tendency for the president’s party to lose House seats during midterm elections. That material did not question the validity of this year’s results. Trump Said He Would Accept 2026 Midterm Results The posts come four days after Trump took a markedly different tone as the scale of Republican losses became apparent. “I am absolutely willing to accept those results,” Trump told the New York Times on election night. “We’ll work with the Democrats, and we’ll, you know, look forward to working with them. We’ll probably work something out.” Trump had been less definitive before Election Day, saying he would accept the outcome if the elections were “honest.” In other election-night remarks, Trump sought to distance himself from the Republican defeat, writing on Truth Social: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” He nevertheless gave Democrats credit for their showing, telling Fox News: “I think the Democrats did a good job. I really do. They fought hard.” Democrats Won House and Senate in Midterm Elections Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday’s elections, dealing Trump and the Republican Party a major setback halfway through his second term. The results included Democratic victories in Republican strongholds and ended unified GOP control of Washington. Democrats have secured at least 54 Senate seats, with two races still unresolved, while flipping more than 40 Republican-held House seats. More than two dozen House races remain uncalled. The House result also came against a historical pattern that Trump himself emphasized after the losses. Since 1946, the president’s party has lost House seats in 18 of 20 midterm elections, with an average loss of about 26 seats. Trump’s Republicans lost 41 House seats during his first midterm election in 2018. The 2026 outcome has already prompted changes inside the administration. White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles is leaving her position, with longtime Trump adviser Stephen Miller named as her replacement, while several senior Justice Department officials have also announced their departures. Election Day Saw Few Major Voting Problems The Associated Press reported that Election Day unfolded with relatively few problems, with the most notable disruptions involving weather and equipment issues in several states. In Westchester County, New York, ballot scanners experienced problems that officials attributed to a programming update, while polling hours were extended at several locations in Pennsylvania and North Carolina following technical issues. The posts Trump shared Saturday questioned whether Democratic vote totals were plausible but did not provide evidence that fraud or other irregularities accounted for Democrats’ victories. The posts mark a notable change in tone just days after Trump’s unusually unambiguous election-night statement that he was prepared to accept the results. Newsweek reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here.
news.summary: Trump shares posts questioning Democratic midterm vote totals, days after saying he was willing to accept the election results.

news.title: The Electoral College May Be The Next Victim Of The 2026 Midterms
news.text:
On Tuesday, Democrats won full control of state government in Pennsylvania, Michigan, Arizona, Wisconsin and Nevada, a shift that could let states effectively bypass the Electoral College before the 2028 presidential election without amending the Constitution.

Those states hold a combined 61 electoral votes. If all five enact the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, the agreement would grow from 222 electoral votes to 283, clearing the 270 it needs to take effect. According to a report from Axios, the Democrats' victories "opened a path to effectively replacing the Electoral College with a national popular vote in time for the 2028 presidential election."

The compact binds member states to award all of their electoral votes to the candidate who wins the national popular vote. That obligation applies even when a member state's own voters choose a different candidate. Once states controlling 270 electoral votes sign on, the agreement would end the possibility of a candidate winning the White House while losing the national popular vote.

Democrats' sweeping statehouse gains have opened a path to effectively replacing the Electoral College with a national popular vote in time for the 2028 presidential election — without needing to amend the Constitution. https://t.co/1WV1WEQxzc— Axios (@axios) November 5, 2026

Americans vote for slates of electors, and those electors choose the president. Nearly every state gives its entire slate to the candidate who carries the state. Maine and Nebraska also award electors by congressional district. The compact keeps the electors in place and changes only the standard member states use to select them, with the switch activating only after membership reaches the 270-vote threshold.

Eighteen states and Washington, D.C. have enacted the compact since organizers launched it in 2006. The member states are California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia and Washington.

Kamala Harris carried every one of those states, along with the District, in the 2024 presidential election. President Trump won the national popular vote that year. Had the compact been in force in 2024, its members would have awarded their electoral votes to Trump.

Ironically, Harris said this summer that Democrats should revisit the Electoral College, among a list of changes she floated that included expanding the Supreme Court and making D.C. and Puerto Rico states.

Nuts... Kamala Harris says if Democrats take back full power they will push to pack the Supreme Court with left-wing activists, abolish the Electoral College, and make DC and Puerto Rico states to add 4 more Democrat Senators.This could destroy America. pic.twitter.com/l8F9Jk0vQx— Steve Cortes (@SteveCortes) October 15, 2026

The compact's supporters rely on Article II, Section 1 of the Constitution, which gives each state's legislature authority to appoint presidential electors "in such Manner as the Legislature thereof may direct." Because that power belongs to the states, backers say they can change how electors are chosen through ordinary state legislation rather than through a constitutional amendment requiring support from two-thirds of both chambers of Congress as well as the high bar of ratification by three-quarters of the states.

Supporters argue that the provision gives states broad discretion over their electors, including the authority to award the state's Electoral College votes to the winner of the national popular vote.

Critics dispute that interpretation, arguing that the Constitution's framers deliberately rejected the idea of electing presidents through a nationwide popular vote. Patrick Valencia, Iowa's deputy solicitor general, argued to NPR that the compact attempts to "usurp the constitutionally required electoral procedures" by keeping the Electoral College technically intact while fundamentally changing how electoral votes are assigned. Critics contend that such a sweeping change to the presidential election system should require a constitutional amendment.

A separate constitutional objection is raised under Article I, Section 10 with respect to interstate compacts and agreements. Opponents of the NPVIC insist it requires congressional approval as it is an agreement which binds the states that are a part of it to a common electoral arrangement which in turn will affect the political power of the states not in the compact. Congress has not approved the agreement.

The central legal issue is whether a state can exercise its constitutional power to appoint electors to effectively convert the Electoral College into a national popular vote system. No court has ever squarely faced that question, and therefore the constitutionality of the compact is still very much in doubt. If it does get to 270 electoral votes and goes into effect, it would be certain to trigger a major constitutional dispute.

news.title: 'Finally, There's a Bit of Hope': UK Officials Eye Iran Peace After US Republicans' Midterm Losses
news.text: British officials accompanying Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the Commonwealth summit in Antigua see a possible opening for Iran peace after Republican midterm defeats. The assessment was reported by The Guardian on Saturday, 7 November 2026, following the elections on Tuesday, 3 November.Democrats secured majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate, ending Republican dominance of the incoming Congress. Republicans nevertheless retain control of the sitting chambers until the new Congress convenes in January 2027.The result may increase pressure on President Donald Trump to pursue negotiations, but no peace agreement has been confirmed.Iran Peace Hopes Grow as London Weighs Midterm ResultsThe mood among British officials shifted as results reached the Commonwealth summit in Antigua. An unnamed government official described unexpected Democratic successes in Kansas, South Carolina and Texas before telling The Guardian, 'Finally, there's a bit of hope.'But the optimism has an economic basis. The US war on Iran has pushed up global energy prices and contributed to higher interest rates, complicating Britain's efforts to ease household costs. Burnham recently acknowledged that his first budget was 'less radical than he had hoped' amid the economic turbulence.Speaking after the election, Burnham said resolving conflict in the Middle East was essential to reducing living costs. He pledged to press other leaders for de-escalation, rather than suggesting negotiations were already under way.Former foreign secretary David Miliband predicted that another assault on Iran might now be less likely and pressure for a settlement stronger. news.title: US anti-trans ballot wins pose challenge for Democrats
news.text:
Voters in four US states approved ballot measures to restrict transgender rights in Tuesday’s midterm elections, sending a warning to Democrats on an issue that has divided the party and is likely to remain a political challenge heading into the 2028 presidential race.

The measures succeeded even as Democrats swept to victorynationwide and retook control of Congress, suggesting voters who backed Democratic candidates were still receptive to some Republican arguments on transgender issues.

Republicans hammered Democrats in midterm campaigns with attack ads painting their opponents as overly liberal on issues like the inclusion of transgender girls in sports, and gender-affirming care for minors.

Democratic candidates were divided in their responses. Some adopted more conservative postures on the issues, some maintained pro-transgender positions and others sidestepped a topic that Republicans wielded effectively against Democrats in the 2024 election.

Voters in Washington, Colorado, Arizona and Nebraska approved ballot measures prohibiting transgender children from playing on sports teams matching their gender identity or banning gender-affirming surgeries for minors.

The success of the ballot measures was “disheartening,” said Rachel Tomlinson Dick, executive director of LGBTQ advocacy group Out Nebraska, adding that they expect to see similar measures on future ballots.

Democrats were caught flat-footed against Republican attacks on transgender issues in the 2024 presidential campaign. The party’s struggle to deliver a coherent response was widely seen as a contributor to former Vice President Kamala Harris’ loss to Trump.

This midterm cycle, candidates responded by emphasizing the need for fairness and rules in sports, which diluted Republican attacks, said Lanae Erickson, senior vice president at Third Way, a think tank that promotes political centrism.

Three of the states that passed anti-trans ballot measures – Washington, Colorado and Arizona – also elected Democrats to a majority of their state and federal seats.

But the success of the measures shows the party still needs to hone a message that appeals to a broad public, Erickson said.

“This week has shown us that Democrats have found effective ways to counter the anti-trans attacks when it comes to candidates, but that doesn’t necessarily mean that they’ve done the work to persuade voters on the issues,” said Erickson, who consulted with Democratic midterm candidates on their approach to transgender issues.

A ​Reuters/Ipsos poll in April found that 67% of survey respondents supported banning transgender people from competing in female school sports. Ninety-two percent of Republicans said they supported such bans, compared with just 44% of Democrats.

Critics warn, however, that moving toward Republicans on trans issues is unlikely to win Democrats new support, and risks alienating LGBTQ voters and the party’s ascendant progressive wing.

The Democratic National Committee did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

MEASURES BAN TRANS ATHLETES, SURGERIES

Some transgender advocates said Tuesday’s electoral outcome was still promising even with the passage of the ballot measures.

The surge of support for Democrats, including some like Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed, who supported transgender rights, showed the limits of the Republican Party’s anti-trans campaign strategy, said Lexi Koren, a communications consultant for No Hate in WA State, a coalition group that opposed Washington’s two ballot measures on trans issues.

“It was a resounding failure,” she said.

Several states including Alabama and Michigan also elected transgender state lawmakers for the first time on Tuesday.

Twenty-seven states had laws in place before Tuesday restricting trans participation in youth sports, according to the nonprofit think tank Movement Advancement Project. That includes Nebraska, whose ballot initiative enshrined the ban in the state constitution.

Two other ballot measures on transgender issues were defeated on Tuesday.

One, in Washington state, would have expanded parental access to school records, potentially enabling parents to learn about a student’s gender identity against the child’s will. Another, in Missouri, would have prohibited gender-affirming care for minors, and also would have repealed the right to abortion.

Even where ballot measures lost, transgender people are still harmed by anti-trans rhetoric proliferating in politics, said Rodrigo Heng-Lehtinen, senior vice president at the Trevor Project, an advocacy group for LGBTQ youth.

“That kind of cultural hostility is not going to go away overnight,” he said.

news.title: Why Democrats Are Crashing Out Over Stephen Miller
news.text:
When President Donald Trump promoted Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff, Democrats started fuming almost instantly. That reaction alone tells you it was a good move.

I suspect Democrats thought the fallout from the midterms would scare Trump into submission. They wanted a chastened president who would spend his final two years tiptoeing around them. Instead, Trump handed the most powerful staff job in Washington to a man they deeply despise, and they read the move as defiance.

They read it correctly.

"Donald Trump learned nothing from his historic defeat. Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration. Trump couldn't have made a worse choice," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) wrote on X shortly after the announcement.

"Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said. "His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor. Fire him today."

“Stephen Miller is a radical ideologue who proudly bolsters a dangerous administration’s worst impulses,” Rep. Chrissy Houlahan (D-Pa.) wrote on X.“Stephen Miller has masterminded the most hateful moments of this Admin. Elevating someone defined by spite and division is a disaster for this country,” Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.) wrote on the site.“Stephen Miller is a white supremacist,” Rep. LaMonica McIver (D-N.J.) said in a statement.“Stephen Miller is the chief architect of Trump’s racist, cruel, and un-American campaign of terror across our country. Innocent people have died and families have been torn apart because of the policies he’s eagerly pushed,” Sen. Catherine Cortez-Masto (D-Nev.) wrote on X.“The American people are begging the White House to focus on lowering costs, but the best Trump can do is ‘more Stephen Miller and the culture of cruelty,’” Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) wrote in a post.

Former deputy press secretary Sarah Matthews, who quit the Trump White House and now makes the rounds as a critic, joined the chorus too.

"The idea that in the last two years of Trump's administration, when he's going to be spiraling because he's a lame-duck president," Matthews told MeidasTouch. "The idea of someone like a Stephen Miller in charge is a very scary thing."

ICYMI: Marjorie Taylor Greene Has a Theory About Trump's Big White House Shake-Up

On Friday, Trump gave Miller the microphone at a Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) event at Mar-a-Lago, and Miller used it to rally Republicans behind the president instead of letting them scatter.

"Let me tell you, if it wasn't for President Trump, the United States of America would not exist right now," Miller said. "This man saved America. He saved our military from collapse. He saved our economy from destruction. He saved our border from annihilation."

Miller highlighted the assassination attempt on Trump's life and the prosecutions he endured. "This man took a bullet for us. He faced down life in prison for us. He saved the Republican Party from the ash heap of history and has made it stronger, more popular, and more resilient than ever before," he said.

Then he made his pledge as chief of staff. "We need to stand with the man who has stood with us and this country with every fiber of his being," Miller added. "It is the honor of my life to be President Trump's chief of staff, and I swear to you, and I pledge to you, Mr. President, my absolute loyalty, my unwavering commitment, and my total devotion to your success and the success of this country."

Stephen Miller just gave his first speech as Chief of Staff to the crowd at @CPAC Mar-A-Lago. He is READY and committed to our nation and our President. I am READY for the era of @StephenM as Chief of Staff! https://t.co/xVuIslH9tr— Joey Mannarino (@JoeyMannarino) November 7, 2026

Miller's speech served as a reminder of what Trump rescued the country from: Joe Biden's incompetence and the destruction carried out by his autopen-wielding staff, which would have rolled right along under Kamala Harris. After a few difficult days for Republicans, Miller reminded the base what's at stake.

Democrats already planned to go to war with this White House, no matter who ran the West Wing. Trump simply decided he'd rather fight that war with a general who won't flinch. A president who caves to his enemies' outrage invites more of it, and Trump has never been that kind of president.

news.title: How Trump Opened the Door for the Christian Left
news.text:
Skip to main content

November 7, 2026

James Talarico on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 in Austin, Texas.

Aaron E. Martinez/The Austin American-Statesman/Getty Images

Two years ago, in the leadup to Kamala Harris’ failed run for president, I spent some time riding around Alabama and Georgia in a big blue tour bus with “Faith, Hope, & Love” plastered prominently along the side. The words come from a phrase in 1 Corinthians. The bus was being chartered by a group called Vote Common Good. The goal of Vote Common Good was to get people to vote for the candidates the group thought most likely to champion the common good — which just so happened to be Democrats, by and large. More specifically, the goal was to be achieved through chipping away at the idea that Republicans had a lock on godliness, that a Republican vote was, indelibly, a vote for God.

The bus was manned by a friendly crew of disaffected evangelicals, barefoot musicians, megachurch outcasts, and racial justice warriors who believed that the Black church in America had gotten politics right, that Jesus’ frequent admonitions to feed the hungry, clothe the poor, and love thy neighbor aligned more with a blue ballot than a red one. As a progressive Christian, I believed firmly in their mission, but I thought it was a mission at the margins. And in some ways, so did they. “We like to tell ourselves we are in a 40-year project,” Doug Pagitt, a Minnesota-based pastor and the organization’s executive director, told me at the time, before going on to explain that while he believed that even a slight change in Evangelical voting patterns could make a difference in some key districts, he had no illusions about wholesale change. It had taken decades to build the Christian Right’s voting bloc. Even Vote Common Good’s most ardent disciples thought they were in for a long slog through the wilderness before they reached anything close to the Promised Land. 

Then came Tuesday’s election results and a parting of the Red Sea right up the I-35 corridor. James Talarico in Texas and Adam Hamilton in Kansas won their deep-red-state Senate elections in a landslide (by 12 and five points, respectively) in part because the Republicans deserved a reckoning, in part because Talarico and Hamilton were highly appealing candidates running against highly unappealing ones, and in part — large part — because their faith-based messaging found footing, especially in states where a majority of the population is church-going.

In fact, Hamilton and Talarico didn’t just provide a permission structure for Christian to make an exception and vote blue; they frequently framed their forays into politics as outgrowths of their faith and their Democratic positions as moral imperatives. On the campaign trail, Hamilton, the chief pastor of the largest church in Kansas and the largest United Methodist congregation in the country, frequently invoked biblical scriptures around fairness, justice, and equality. “I see a lot of people claiming to be Christians, and I wonder, ‘What Gospels are you reading?’” he told CBS. Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian, has defended gun control, LGBTQ rights and abortion access — not in spite of biblical teachings but in fact because of them — and has proven a perfect religious counterpoint to authoritarian stances and Christian nationalism of his opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. “When I open my Bible, I don’t see any verses about abortion, but I see more than 2000 verses about economic justice. I don’t see any verses about gay marriage, but I see hundreds of verses about welcoming the stranger and feeding the hungry and healing the sick and freeing the oppressed,” Talarico told me back in 2024. “There [has been] a concerted effort to move Christians away from the gospel and toward right-wing political objectives, but there’s very little scriptural basis for the agenda of Christian nationalist politicians in this country. Christian nationalists want us to think that Christianity is about dominating our neighbors, winning at all costs, indoctrinating children. Christians have a moral obligation to speak out against this perversion of our faith.” 

These are the types of arguments that have long been made by the Christian left, but were mostly drowned out in primaries long before they came close to reaching the national stage. And, ironically, without Trump, that trend may well have continued. Which is to say that in just a few years, the president’s profound corruption, incompetence, cruelty, and pandering to the religious right accomplished what otherwise may have taken generations: It opened a door for the religious left to make incredible inroads.

The smartest thing the Democrats could do is endeavor to keep that door open. To maintain control in a blessedly post-Trump future, the party will need a unifying strategy beyond opposition to just one man. They will need a vision that moves beyond wedge issues and a coalition that is not dogmatic (and yes, I realize the irony in using this word). They will need, quite literally, some faith — by which I mean faith voters. “One of the big lessons of this election is that Democrats can expand the democracy-supporting coalition by including people of faith,” Pagitt, the Minnesota pastor, tells me. “The answer is not to make the party more religious, or to rely on running religious candidates. The goal is significant outreach to the many communities that make up the fabric of our society, and real inclusion of them.”

This does not mean randomly posting Bible verses about the Lord’s power “that is at work within us,” as Hakeem Jeffries did in the wake of the election. It does not mean trying to beat the religious right at their own game and reaching for some form of performative Christian nationalism-lite. But it likely does mean putting forth more candidates whose values seem unassailable, and hewed to something other than the party itself. These values don’t need to come from religion, of course, but Tuesday’s election proves that it might not hurt the Democrats if sometimes they did. According to a recent Pew Research center poll, a majority of Americans believe in separation of church and state, and yet a majority also say that religion plays a positive role in society. Sixty-three percent of Democrats reported having a net positive view of religion (38 percent) or a neutral one (25 percent). For candidates whose faith is authentic — who don’t want to legislate their beliefs but who aren’t afraid to say that their morality is grounded in them — that faith could be seen as a bulwark against political transgressions, the selling out of the very people one is meant to represent.

Indeed, America has a long and proud history of progressive Christians using the power of their faith to make life better for people in the here and now, from operating stops on the Underground Railroad to fighting against poverty, child labor, domestic abuse, and war. Here, there is a long and proud tradition of a social gospel that focuses on healing the actual world rather than storing up mansions in heaven with adherence to a hard-line, fundamentalist worldview, one in which extremism trumps love and human suffering hastens Jesus’ Second Coming. Though it hasn’t been the dominant religious narrative in Trump’s America, Talarico and Hamilton belong to that long and proud tradition. And that’s a second coming millions of voters would rejoice to see.

news.title: Young Conservatives Have A New Mascot, And He’s A Sith Lord
news.text:
With Republicans having brutally lost Congress after Tuesday’s midterm elections, young conservatives on the internet are glorifying the authoritarian and genocidal actions of a new mascot, made famous in the “Star Wars” space opera movie franchise.

The fictional Jedi Knight Anakin Skywalker — who eventually embraces evil to become iconic villain Darth Vader — has emerged as an unlikely political icon among young right-wing internet users, who are posting to social media memes and dramatic video edits celebrating his descent into authoritarianism. The trend, which predates the 2026 midterms, reflects growing resentment toward established institutions, generational divides, and dissatisfaction with modern society, according to Know Your Meme, which refers to the phenomenon as “Anakin Skywalker Gen Z Male Rage Memes.” (RELATED: Manifest Destiny Is Born Again Among Young Conservatives On Social Media)

Young white men, a demographic which helped fuel President Donald Trump’s 2024 victory, turned elsewhere in the midterms, backing Democratic House candidates by a 10-point margin. White voters under 30 years of age supported Democrats 61% to 36%, reversing their 2024 preference for Trump, who won 54% of the demographic compared to then-Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris’s 44%, according to Tufts University.

The trend, sometimes called “Anakin-maxxing,” gained traction throughout October as younger users began comparing their frustrations with the Republican Party to Skywalker’s increasingly bitter relationship with the seemingly rigid Jedi Council.

One compilation of such memes posted by an Austrian conservative account on X shows a wide variety of topics, from mass migration to transgenderism and even economic collapse.

One of the “Anakin-maxxing” memes posted by the conservative X account “Necromancer” references the infamous attack on USS Liberty by Israeli forces, alluding to it as forbidden knowledge “not a story the Republicans would tell you.”

Israeli fighter jets and torpedo boats attacked the USS Liberty, an American intelligence-gathering vessel operating in international waters during the 1967 Six-Day War, on June 8, killing 34 Americans and wounding 171, according to the U.S. Navy. Several former senior American intelligence officials, including two former National Security Agency directors, have argued the attack was deliberate, according to the U.S. Naval Institute, although Israel maintains its forces mistakenly identified the American vessel as an Egyptian ship, according to State Department records.

One of the Anakin-focused memes posted by The Blaze columnist Auron MacIntyre makes fun of claims by baby boomers that obstacles to personal economic advancement are related to Gen Z’s eating habits.

If you wanted to own a house before 40 you should have never ate that burrito Anakin https://t.co/ofcuZK3ugC— Auron MacIntyre (@AuronMacintyre) November 2, 2026

The online fascination also mirrors an earlier wave of American empire memes celebrating expansionism and military power among young conservatives.

Baby boomers themselves also tend to be a common subject targeted by the memes. One post, made by X account “WhodatJoey,” highlights the disparity in economic splendor which baby boomers lived in compared with the less rosy one affecting Gen Z.

One early X post made by a Norwegian identified as Aleksander Ætelmann depicts Skywalker burning on the fictional volcanic planet Mustafar, accompanied by grievances about college debt, pandemic restrictions, artificial intelligence threatening jobs, and unaffordable rent.

The fictional character’s appeal is rooted in his transformation from an idealistic young Jedi serving the bureaucratic Galactic Republic into a ruthless servant of the succeeding Galactic Empire. Many online-using conservatives view this phenomenon as an allegory of how optimistic they themselves were about the future before becoming disillusioned and disenfranchised by Republicans’ apparently broken promises to improve their lives.

The trend of posts get darker, eventually evenly embracing fascism as a supposed solution to corruption in governments throughout the world. One example of this is seen in a post made by the X account BlockPresto.

Other young conservatives, however, apparently see things differently.

Such young right-wingers identify with Skywalker’s resentment toward an older political establishment which refuses to recognize his abilities, according to an October 17 X post by commentator Connor Tomlinson.

Their interpretation also goes beyond merely sympathizing with a fictional villain.

The prequel trilogy of “Star Wars” movies can be understood as a story about a young man whose idealism is exploited by corrupt institutions, leaving him vulnerable to the evil he originally opposed, conservative commentator Kangmin Lee argued in an October 26 X post.

The trend has produced a generational dispute within conservative circles.

After commentator Matt Walsh criticized the prequel trilogy’s writing and acting, social media users began depicting him as Ki-Adi-Mundi, an older Jedi Council member skeptical of Skywalker, according to Know Your Meme.

Some of the memes touch on the Great Replacement, the process by which white people are replaced throughout the West by third-worlders, exemplified in a post by the X account “Banished Lion.”

The phenomenon has even attracted the attention of prominent political figures.

An image depicting an imagined, noncanonical ending in which Skywalker rules the Galactic Empire alongside his family was shared by billionaire Elon Musk, who captioned his Nov. 1 post, “This is what they stole from us.”

This is what they stole from us https://t.co/q1GnpjF394— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 1, 2026

Whether Skywalker’s newfound admirers genuinely embrace authoritarian politics or simply enjoy provocative internet humor remains difficult to establish.

The character’s transformation, however, offers an uncomfortable irony: the young man who believed he could fix a broken political system ultimately helped destroy it.

“So this is how liberty dies. With thunderous applause,” Padmé, Skywalker’s soon-to-be-killed wife, famously remarked as the fictional Emperor Sheev Palpatine declared the creation of the Galactic Empire. Skywalker, as Darth Vader, however, is ultimately redeemed in the saga’s sixth film and seemingly destroys the evil to which he succumbed.

news.title: US Anti-Trans Ballot Wins Pose Challenge for Democrats Ahead of 2028
news.text: Washington: Voters in four US states approved ballot measures to restrict transgender rights in Tuesday's midterm elections, sending a warning to Democrats on an issue ​that has divided the party and is likely to remain a political challenge heading into the 2028 presidential race.The measures succeeded even as ‌Democrats swept to victorynationwide and retook control of Congress, suggesting voters who backed Democratic candidates were still receptive to some Republican arguments on transgender issues.Republicans hammered Democrats in midterm campaigns with attack ads painting their opponents as overly liberal on issues like the inclusion of transgender girls in sports, and gender-affirming care for minors.Democratic candidates were divided in their responses. Some adopted more conservative postures on the issues, some maintained ​pro-transgender positions and others sidestepped a topic that Republicans wielded effectively against Democrats in the 2024 election.Voters in Washington, Colorado, Arizona and Nebraska approved ballot ​measures prohibiting transgender children from playing on sports teams matching their gender identity or banning gender-affirming surgeries for minors.The success of the ⁠ballot measures was "disheartening," said Rachel Tomlinson Dick, executive director of LGBTQ advocacy group Out Nebraska, adding that they expect to see similar measures on future ballots.Democrats were caught ​flat-footed against Republican attacks on transgender issues in the 2024 presidential campaign. The party's struggle to deliver a coherent response was widely seen as a contributor to former Vice ​President Kamala Harris' loss to Trump.This midterm cycle, candidates responded by emphasizing the need for fairness and rules in sports, which diluted Republican attacks, said Lanae Erickson, senior vice president at Third Way, a think tank that promotes political centrism.Three of the states that passed anti-trans ballot measures - Washington, Colorado and Arizona - also elected Democrats to a majority of their state and federal seats.Fixed income can still offer valuable protection. So are bonds back to having your portfolios back?But the success ​of the measures shows the party still needs to hone a message that appeals to a broad public, Erickson said."This week has shown us that Democrats have found ​effective ways to counter the anti-trans attacks when it comes to candidates, but that doesn’t necessarily mean that they’ve done the work to persuade voters on the issues," said Erickson, who consulted ‌with Democratic midterm candidates ⁠on their approach to transgender issues.A Reuters/Ipsos poll in April found that 67% of survey respondents supported banning transgender people from competing in female school sports. Ninety-two percent of Republicans said they supported such bans, compared with just 44% of Democrats.Critics warn, however, that moving toward Republicans on trans issues is unlikely to win Democrats new support, and risks alienating LGBTQ voters and the party's ascendant progressive wing.The Democratic National Committee did not immediately respond to a request for comment.MEASURES BAN TRANS ATHLETES, SURGERIESSome transgender advocates said Tuesday's electoral ​outcome was still promising even with the ​passage of the ballot measures.The surge ⁠of support for Democrats, including some like Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed, who supported transgender rights, showed the limits of the Republican Party's anti-trans campaign strategy, said Lexi Koren, a communications consultant for No Hate in WA State, a coalition group that opposed Washington's two ballot ​measures on trans issues."It was a resounding failure," she said.Several states including Alabama and Michigan also elected transgender state lawmakers ​for the first time ⁠on Tuesday.Twenty-seven states had laws in place before Tuesday restricting trans participation in youth sports, according to the nonprofit think tank Movement Advancement Project. That includes Nebraska, whose ballot initiative enshrined the ban in the state constitution.Two other ballot measures on transgender issues were defeated on Tuesday.One, in Washington state, would have expanded parental access to school records, potentially enabling parents ⁠to learn ​about a student's gender identity against the child's will. Another, in Missouri, would have prohibited gender-affirming care for minors, ​and also would have repealed the right to abortion.Even where ballot measures lost, transgender people are still harmed by anti-trans rhetoric proliferating in politics, said Rodrigo Heng-Lehtinen, senior vice president at the Trevor Project, an advocacy ​group for LGBTQ youth."That kind of cultural hostility is not going to go away overnight," he said.

news.title: Trump deserved US midterm defeat – Kemi Badenoch
news.text:
British Conservative Party leader, Kemi Badenoch, has said United States President Donald Trump deserved to be defeated in the country’s midterm elections, criticising his handling of the Iran war, trade policies and treatment of allies, The Independent reports on Saturday.

Badenoch described Trump’s electoral setback as “entirely self-inflicted” and condemned what she called his “dirty” style of politics in an interview with The Independent Editor-in-Chief, Geordie Greig.

The Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections, flipping at least seven Senate seats and more than two dozen House districts in a major setback for Trump’s Republican Party.

Asked whether Trump deserved the defeat, Badenoch replied, “Yeah. He has not been acting in the way that I would consider conservative.”

She criticised his tariffs, threats towards Canada and Greenland, and disputes with US allies, saying his actions contradicted conservative principles of free markets and better trade.

“Where is the push for free markets and better trade… rather than protectionism, America first, the squabbling with allies? That’s not what conservatives do,” she said.

Badenoch also criticised Trump’s personal attacks on journalists and political figures, saying his conduct fell below the standards expected of a statesman.

“Trump is very charming in person, but you see the way that he talks about journalists, about individuals. It doesn’t meet the standards a statesman should meet – always wanting to get dirty in terms of insults and so on,” she said.

She said she was particularly unhappy with Trump’s remarks about British Prime Minister Keir Starmer and described his treatment of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at the White House as “awful”. 

On the Iran war, Badenoch said she understood Trump’s initial decision to launch the military action, which she supported because of concerns about Iran acquiring nuclear weapons, but questioned the absence of a clear strategy.

“We don’t want them getting nuclear weapons. But where’s the plan?” she asked.

She also said she would have been content if Trump had lost the 2024 presidential election to his Democratic opponent, Kamala Harris.

Asked which of the two candidates she preferred, Badenoch said, “I would say I like them both equally. Make of that what you will.”

The Conservative leader also argued that Trump had squandered the broad coalition of voters that helped him win the presidency, including Latino voters and more Black voters than any previous Republican candidate.

“What’s the first thing he does? Tariffs, and then talking about Greenland and Canada. A lot of people were wondering, ‘What are you doing?’” she said.

Badenoch’s comments came amid wider criticism of Trump’s handling of the economy and foreign policy following the Republicans’ losses in the midterms.

Badenoch is the leader of the UK Conservative Party and Leader of the Opposition. She became Conservative leader in November 2024 after defeating Robert Jenrick in the party’s leadership contest. She previously served as the UK’s Business and Trade Secretary and Minister for Women and Equalities under former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak.

Badenoch, whose birth name is Olukemi Olufunto Adegoke, was born in Wimbledon, London, in 1980 to Nigerian parents.

news.title: Joel Kotkin: MAGA is wounded. Here’s how Carney should respond
news.text:
The MAGA wipeout has been greeted abroad as something of both a humiliation of President Donald Trump and the beginning of “normal” politics. Foreign leaders from Tehran to Brussels could hardly contain their glee. 

Yet this should not be taken, as some may hope, as a permanent victory for the liberal globalist worldview that dominated during the Obama years. People, particularly today, are more likely to vote against someone, or a party, than for them. It was detestation of Hillary Clinton and then Kamala Harris that allowed the never widely popular Trump to get into office. 

Yet if MAGA is gone, the forces that drove it will not disappear. Voters may not like the excesses of Homeland Security, but they definitely do not want to return to Biden’s open borders policy. Nor is there a popular demand for a ban on fossil fuels or for allowing males to compete in women’s sports. None of this will change.
