news.title: New pope, rise of Luke Littler and what that has happened since Spurs last won four games in a row
news.text:
It has been 1,108 days since Tottenham last won four Premier League games in a row - a run they could end this weekend when they face Leeds at Elland Road.

Not since the opening months of Ange Postecoglou’s reign have Spurs won more than three times in succession - a feat they quickly achieved twice either side of a north London derby draw under the Australian between August and October 2023 - and a lot has happened in the intervening three years.

That season, fast-starting Tottenham won eight of their first 10 fixtures and went five points clear at the summit despite the high-profile summer loss of Harry Kane to Bayern Munich, eventually finishing in fifth place.

Here, Standard Sport looks at some of the biggest stories to have happened since Spurs last won four on the bounce.

Cardinal Robert Francis Prevost was elected as the 267th Pope of the Catholic Church in May 2025, taking the name Pope Leo XIV.

While Pope Leo is said to be a Real Madrid fan, he was gifted a Sunderland shirt with the name "Pope Leo, 14" emblazoned on the back ahead of the club’s Europa League campaign.

Pope Leo was gifted the shirt after Sunderland’s chaplain, Father Marc Lyden-Smith, gave one to Pope Francis ahead of the Black Cats’ victory over Newcastle in 2013.

Donald Trump was re-elected as President of the United States in November 2024, defeating Democratic candidate and former vice-president Kamala Harris.

It came four years after Mr Trump had lost the 2020 election to Joe Biden, ending his initial spell in the White House after victory over Hillary Clinton in 2016.

The Labour Party came back into power after 14 years as Sir Keir Starmer was elected as UK Prime Minister in July 2024.

Despite a landslide victory, Starmer resigned in July 2026 and was replaced by Andy Burnham.

The UK has now had five Prime Ministers in the last five years.

Daniel Levy stepped down as executive chairman of Tottenham in September 2025, bringing to an end his 25-year reign at the club.

Following Levy’s departure, non-executive chairman Peter Charrington declared “a new era of leadership for the club” before Spurs went on to endure their worst season in Premier League history as they only narrowly avoided relegation to the Championship on the final day.

Tottenham would have been relegated had they not mustered up a nervy 1-0 win at home to Everton on the final day of last season.

12 months after lifting the Europa League, their first major trophy for 17 years, Spurs would remarkably become mired in a relegation battle with rivals West Ham, staying up by the skin of their teeth thanks to a goal from loanee Joao Palhinha.

Spurs’ decision to get rid of Postecoglou just 16 days after he guided them to Europa League success over Manchester United in Bilbao was always going to prove controversial.

No one, though, could have foreseen the disaster that would unfurl over the next season as Tottenham went through three managerial changes in 10 months.

Thomas Frank was brought in as Postecoglou’s successor, but was eventually sacked in February 2026 with the club hovering over the relegation zone.

His replacement, Igor Tudor, lasted just 44 days before the club hit the panic button again to bring in Roberto De Zerbi to steer them to safety.

In the space of three years, West Ham went from Conference League winners to being relegated to the Championship.

A series of poor recruitment decisions, managerial changes and ownership uncertainty ensured the Hammers failed to build on their first piece of major silverware in 43 years before eventually dropping back to the second tier after 14 seasons.

Darts sensation Luke Littler announced himself on the biggest stage at just 16 years old as he made a historic run to the World Championship final on his debut at Alexandra Palace in January 2024.

Since then, Littler has become a back-to-back world champion and underlined his place as the best player on the planet while still a teenager.

Another sporting prodigy, Kimi Antonelli has risen from obscurity to the top of his sport in the last three years.

At just 20 years and 68 days old, Kimi Antonelli became the youngest Formula One world champion in history on Sunday after clinching the 2026 title with a third-place finish at the Mexico City Grand Prix.

A record-breaking campaign has also seen Antonelli become the youngest winner of the Monaco Grand Prix, the youngest driver to achieve a Grand Slam, and the first Italian in more than 60 years to be crowned world champion.

Sir Andy Murray and Rafael Nadal retired within a few months of each other to leave Novak Djokovic as the last man standing from the ‘Big Four’ era of 21st century tennis.

Two-time Wimbledon winner Murray retired in August 2024 and was swiftly followed by 22-time Grand Slam champion Nadal in October. It followed Roger Federer’s retirement in September 2022.

Boxing fans have long since grown weary of Tyson Fury’s retirement U-turns, so his fourth announcement last year that he was hanging up his gloves convinced few. Just a handful of months later, he made the decision to step back into the ring for a fifth, and surely, final time in April 2026.

The former world heavyweight champion beat Russian Arslanbek Makhmudov by unanimous decision in his first fight back and is now gearing up for a hotly-anticipated bout with Anthony Joshua in Cardiff in December, having also defeated Mariusz Wach in Thailand.
news.summary: It has been over three years since Spurs won four Premier League games in a row

news.title: 'Dirty' Trump deserved to be thrashed in the US midterms, says Kemi Badenoch
news.text:
Kemi Badenoch says Donald Trump 'deserved to be thrashed' in the US elections and has denounced his 'dirty' style of politics.

In a sweeping attack on the American President's record she criticised him over the Iran War, for threatening Canada and Greenland, imposing swingeing tariffs and “squabbling with allies” like the UK.

Trump's heavy defeat in the US mid term elections was “entirely self inflicted”, she told The Independent Editor-in-Chief Geordie Greig.

Controversially, Badenoch said she would have been content if Trump had never won a second term in the White House and his Democrat opponent, Left winger Kamala Harris had become President in 2024 instead.

In the wide-ranging exclusive interview for The Talk Show, Badenoch also savaged Tory predecessors Boris Johnson and Liz Truss for their “mistakes” in government.

She said Andy Burnham was more “fun” than Keir Starmer, but behind the “charm” he was “dangerous.”

She called Nigel Farage's Reform Party “bonkers” and ruled out serving in a Conservative-Reform Coalition led by him.

But she conceded that before his dip in popularity, Farage had made an “emotional connection” with voters that the Tories had lost until she became leader.

Badenoch's outspoken condemnation of Trump's policies and personality may come as a surprise, especially to Tory supporters, some of whom urged her to copy him after he won power. 

Asked if he deserved to be thrashed, she did not hesitate: “Yeah. He has not been acting in the way that I would consider conservative. Where is the push for free markets and better trade... rather than protectionism, America first, the squabbling with allies? That's not what conservatives do.

“Trump is very charming in person, but you see the way that he talks about journalists, about individuals. It doesn't meet the standards a statesman should meet - always wanting to get dirty in terms of insults and and so on.

“When he was rude about Keir Starmer... I didn't like that at all. What they did to President Zelensky in the White House was awful.”

Trump had won power “with an extraordinary coalition of Latinos, more Black voters than any other Republican” - and wasted it. 

“What's the first thing he does? Tariffs, and then talking about Greenland and Canada. A lot of people were wondering, ‘what are you doing?’”

She understood Trump's initial decision to go to war with Iran - which she had backed. 

“We don't want them getting nuclear weapons. But where's the plan?”

Join us as an Independent member and support our journalism for just £1 . Sign up here

His defeat in the mid term elections was “entirely self-inflicted”, she said. “Voters want results.”

Ms Badenoch claimed she would have been happy if Trump had lost the last presidential election - and revealed a hitherto unknown admiration for fellow black female politician Kamala Harris.

“People ask me who did I prefer, Kamala Harris, Donald Trump? I would say I like them both equally. Make of that what you will.”

While refusing to 'name and blame' former Conservative PMs Johnson and Truss, she was fiercely critical of both their records in No 10. They were guilty of “gimmicks, mistakes and short termism. Everybody made mistakes. Obviously, the leaders were responsible for most of them. Immigration was too high.”

Did she mean Johnson and the so called 'Boris wave' of immigration? 

“People know who the prime minister was then,” she said, removing all doubt.

Truss got equally short shrift. Badenoch savaged the disastrous budget that saw Truss kicked out of Downing Street after six weeks.

“You can't just announce £150 billion bailing out people's energy bills and £45 billion of tax cuts with no spending cuts at all,” she said disbelievingly. 

“Those are the wrong way of doing things.”

Rather than call out Johnson and Truss personally, Badenoch, a Methodist, quoted St Augustine: “Hate the sin, love the sinner.”

She deflected the notion that Burnham's “charm” has revived Labour fortunes since awkward Starmer's demise.

Calling him a “foot in mouth” politician, she says: “He says things first and then thinks about it later.”

He is more genial. I'm not sure I would call it charm. He looks like he'd be more fun company at a party, (but) that makes him more dangerous because he wants to please everybody.”

With the latest polls indicating the Conservatives have narrowed the gap with Labour to two points, she insists she has his measure, boasting: “The more Andy Burnham sees of me, the less he wants to have an early election.”

She is equally confident about seeing off the challenge from Farage, whose ratings have fallen in the wake of a series of scandals to hit him and Reform. It has coincided with the Conservatives overtaking Reform in the political ratings war.

“At the moment, I am beating him, and I think he's very worried about that.”

She freely admitted Farage initially struck a chord with the public at a time the Tories were floundering. 

“What worked for him was having an emotional connection and an authenticity which we as a party had lost, sounding very technocratic.”

That had all changed now she was Tory leader and the shine was coming off Farage. 

“One of the things going wrong for him was that he pretended to be this everyman. 

“A lot of his supporters... don't understand how he's getting £5 million and they're not able to pay their energy bills.”

It was up to a Commons inquiry to decide if Farage's £5 million donation from a crypto currency billionaire was “corrupt”, said Badenoch. But she has made up her mind. 

“His story doesn't add up.”

She is just as adamant she would never serve under 'Prime Minister Farage.'

“No, because he would not be good for this country. I simply wouldn't.”

Some of Reform's ideas, such as a recent proposal to ‘nationalise Poundland' were plain “bonkers”.

She claimed Farage did her a favour with the acrimonious defection of defeated Tory leadership rival Robert Jenrick to Reform earlier this year.

Getting rid of Jenrick was like defusing an “unexploded bomb” - leaks from the Shadow Cabinet ceased overnight, she said.

Badenoch joked: “The only thing I haven't done is written a thank you card to Nigel Farage for taking these problems away. I'll write it in his Christmas card!”

She defended her aggressive style at the Commons despatch box.

“You have to be a fighter to survive. There are 400 Labour MPs screaming and shouting. I need to put some of those people in their place. It's a kill or be killed arena.”

Which explains why she refused to say sorry for calling ex Education Secretary Bridget Phillipson “spiteful” for the closure of private schools as a result of Labour's VAT on school fees. 

“Spiteful. What's wrong with that?” she retorted.

“She hurt many, many children. They had to leave their schools, which closed down. It was class war. So yes, I will call it like it is.

“We've spent a lot of time dressing things up in fancy words where most of the public don't understand what we're talking about.”

After putting a difficult start as Conservative leader behind her, Ms Badenoch said Labour and Reform jibes do not get under her thick skin. Even if they did she would not show it.

She is proud of being a 'cool customer,' adding: “I'm a poker player. I have a very good poker face.

“I remember saying to some people I get better every day, and they mocked it. But it's true. I believe in continuous improvement.”
news.summary: In a wide-ranging and revealing exclusive interview for The Talk Show with Geordie Greig, Badenoch also savaged Tory predecessors Boris Johnson and Liz Truss for their ‘mistakes’ in government

'I was cock-a-hoop in 2024. But that glorious Trump presidential win seems a long time ago'

It is a long way back for the Republicans. 

7.01am, 7 Nov 2026

Share options

WHEN DONALD J Trump was elected President of the United States for a second but not consecutive term in 2024 I was cock-a-hoop. Such joy!

The Americans had thoroughly rejected DEI Harris, and the sunny uplands of steady economic growth, the rejection of woke nonsense and an end to stupid foreign wars lay ahead.

Sure, Trump is unconventional and unpredictable, but you hope for the best.

After the blue tsunami of the midterm elections on Tuesday, that glorious Trump presidential win seems a long time ago.

Conservatives should not underestimate the scale of the loss. Wins for the Democratic Party included Senate seats in Texas, Kansas and South Carolina and the governorship of Texas, all for the first time in decades.

In 2024, Trump carried Texas by 13.7 percentage points, Kansas by 16.1 and South Carolina by 17.9. As of 5 November, Democrats flipped seven Republican-held Senate seats, bringing the Democratic caucus to 54 seats, including two independents.

Abdul El-Sayed, a left-wing Democratic candidate, took the Senate race in Michigan against Mike Rogers. In Maine, Democrats won the Senate seat from Republican incumbent Susan Collins, who had held it for almost 30 years.

Trump put together an amazing coalition to win the presidency in 2024 which included taking the popular vote by 2.3 million votes. Hispanic men broke substantially in his favour, and of course young, white working class men were his base (many called him Daddy) and white women without a college degree strongly supported Trump, with more than 60% voting for him. He increased his vote among African Americans although overall they voted overwhelmingly for Harris.

The Trump coalition was similar to the one that Robert F Kennedy was pulling together for his presidential run in 1968, before he was struck down by an assassin’s bullet. Pat Buchanan, a Republican, also tried to build a similar coalition, eating away at the Democrats’ traditional working-class base. In fact, Buchanan was the first Republican to use the phrase America First in 1992.

Advertisement

But coalitions, by their very nature, are fragile. They consist by definition of differing groups with different identities. Once-in-a-generation charismatic figures can bring these groups of working class men and women with diverse identities, who love their country, together under a unifying vision. Trump’s message was simple: he would put America First. Trump’s slogan of ”Kamala is for they/them, President Trump is for you” was seen as campaign defining. 

It turns out President Trump put Trump first.

The months rolled by and the whiff of corruption grew stronger, the talk of ballrooms grew bolder. This, I believe, would have been tolerated (or priced in) if the economy had remained strong.

Trump decided against that, slapping tariffs on goods and finally starting a ruinous war against Iran. The president failed to secure regime change in Iran; he got regime range in Texas instead.

MAGA can blame woke, leftist women all they want, but the Iran war, and its consequences were a major concern for American voters.

Indeed, a Fox News survey showed 75% of respondents were either “extremely” (42%) or “very” (33%) concerned about the war in Iran.

According to the AP-NORC poll, 62% of registered voters named the war as one of the most important issues, and a further 31% said it was “an important issue, but not one of the most important”.

The Fox poll further found that six in 10 voters oppose US military action against Iran.

As early as June this year outlets such as the Daily Beast were running headlines such as ’Trump voters turn against him over ‘terrible’ gas prices’ and ‘Americans are paying more for gas now than at any point over the last four years’. The vice-president also blamed the war in Iran for the crushing defeat.

Indeed, the Maine Morning Star reported on 30 October 2026, that ‘Heating oil now 82% more expensive than this time last year’. The piece explained “the average price for heating oil reached a new high this week at $6.05 a gallon, according to the Maine Department of Energy Resources. That means it will cost roughly $750 more to fill a standard 275-gallon oil tank”. That $750 dollars might not be much to Trump or Elon Musk, but it is a huge amount for the average voter in Maine.

This week voters in Maine elected a Democrat to the Senate for the first time in 30 years.

Trump's grip on America is broken, but he could be more dangerous now

I was at Talarico's watch party as he 'took back Texas'. Here's what it was like

Since Vietnam, American voters are sceptical of foreign wars on their own terms. When these wars are a direct cause of increasing domestic energy prices, on top of tariffs, they will punish whoever started that war. American presidential candidates nearly always promise to stay out of foreign wars and yet once elected repeatedly they get dragged into them. 

I suspect once the presidents are sworn in and the generals start pointing out all the shiny toys at the tip of their fingers, presidents seem to turn into eight-year-old boys once again, playing soldiers. Resistance is futile.

President Kennedy was dragged into Vietnam, although he did avert an actual nuclear war only months before. President Johnson was desperate to end the war in Vietnam, a war that destroyed his presidency, but that passed to Nixon.

President Bush Sr launched the first Iraq war, President George W Bush launched the war in Afghanistan and the second Iraq war. In Vietnam, Afghanistan and Iraq 2, the Americans eventually cut and ran. America has many admirable virtues, the ability to wage war to any purpose is not one of them.

President Trump is still at war in Iran, although without soldiers on the ground. He now needs an exit route, which will be difficult to find.

The Republicans can still put together a convincing campaign for 2028, but they will struggle to put together the same coalition of voters as 2024.

Coalitions need to be nurtured, not ignored; their interests must be protected, not sacrificed to presidential whims and dreams of a foreign war.

It is a long way back for the Republicans. 

Laura Perrins is a mother of four and writes on Substack at The West Brit

news.summary: It is a long way back for the Republicans.

news.title: Don't be fooled, the defeat of Trump doesn't mean the end of Maga
news.text:
This is Dispatches with Patrick Cockburn, a subscriber-only newsletter from The i Paper. If you’d like to get this direct to your inbox, every single week, you can sign up here.

The US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February confident they could achieve regime change. By an extraordinary irony, eight months later the greatest regime-change taking place as a result of the war is in Washington, not Tehran. 

Donald Trump’s administration is not sinking with all hands, but it is visibly holed below the waterline, its chief member demoralised and fights breaking out over who to blame for its electoral calamity.

To a degree, all governments depend for their authority on bluffing and frightening everybody into believing that they are all-powerful and able to ignore puny efforts to resist them. Nothing exposes this masquerade as swiftly and humiliatingly as an unsuccessful war waged against a smaller and weaker opponent.

History is full of supposed turning points when the political world turns out not to have turned quite as much as observers had expected. But I suspect that this will not prove true of the US midterm elections just past, when the greatest global power moved decisively in one direction when it might have gone another way.

During my career as a foreign correspondent, I have watched democratic and semi-democratic states, such as Russia in 1999 and Turkey in 2016, turn into full-blown dictatorships. I understand how swiftly and irrevocably this can occur – and in the last two years America was fast going the same way. 

Trump may appear to be a uniquely American phenomenon, yet his actions mirrored all the classic moves by which modern-day populist dictators, like Vladimir Putin in Russia and Recep Tayyip Erdoğan in Turkey, established autocratic rule. They hold nominally free elections but have enough influence over them to ensure they never lose. Republicans now point to the swingeing losses as proof this never happened, but if it did not, it was not for lack of trying right up to election day. 

In the last 18 months, Trump made multiple efforts to in effect steal the midterms – something he falsely accused Joe Biden of doing in the presidential election in 2020. He put his full authority behind a Republican campaign to gerrymander congressional districts to his party’s advantage, which, without the Iran war generating a Democratic landslide, might well have been an election-winning ploy. 

His campaign to control the election machinery was ruthlessly fought on many fronts. Walter Olson of the Cato Institute writes that from March 2025, Trump signed multiple executive orders that “asserted sweeping powers over elections that neither the Constitution nor Congress had assigned to presidents”. 

Dozens of lawsuits were filed to compel election officials, through threat of criminal prosecution, to submit voter rolls to be inspected and purged by Washington. Trump had an ultimately abortive plan to appoint proxies to run the US Postal Service who would decide who could vote by mail. With 24 million voters in the midterms – 20 per cent of the total – using mail-in ballots, this and other measures had the potential to swing an election had they not been blocked by the lower courts.

Already the outcome of the midterms begins to feel inevitable, so that people may forget – and the Republicans dearly hope they will forget – that up until a few months ago their strenuous efforts to fix the election might have worked.

Yet obituaries of Trumpism are premature, with 53 per cent of white males – rising to 63 per cent for those without a college degree – voting Republican, according to an NBC exit poll. Some 24 per cent of all voters still identify with Maga and 82 per cent of evangelical Christians stayed firmly in the Trump camp. While 62 per cent of voters disapprove of the President, it is still shocking to find that, after two years of brutal, incompetent, corrupt government by Trump, about 38 per cent of voters still approve of him.

Much of Trump’s famous “base” stays loyal, but the all-important magic of invincibility is gone. Populist nationalist movements may differ from country to country, but they all have a cult of the supreme leader, from Narendra Modi in India today to Benito Mussolini in Italy a century ago. Most “strongmen” or Latin American caudillos have feet of clay, but nothing exposes this like a failed war.

Vice-President JD Vance is certainly correct in saying this is the overriding explanation for Republican defeat, but it is too late to do much about it. Conceivably, Trump might opt for one last throw of the dice and start a third round of his war with Iran, but he and Vance have been ruling this out in recent days. 

The only time the Republicans recovered briefly in the polls over the summer was during the short-lived peace deal – or memorandum of understanding – with Iran, and when it collapsed so did Republican support. Vance adds that to win back voters, the White House must prioritise distancing itself from Israel, showing how far the geopolitical map has been transformed by the war.

America dodged the authoritarian bullet almost accidentally thanks to a failed war – but it came perilously close.

Further Thoughts

Ability as an orator was once considered to be an essential skill for a politician. Speeches by leaders like Abraham Lincoln were reported verbatim in local newspapers long before he became US president. The same was true of Liberal leader WE Gladstone in Britain. I assume that radio and television played a role in killing this skill off because they reported only soundbites.

Our expectations of speakers are now very low. I remember a speech by Sir Keir Starmer to the Labour Party Conference in 2025 bulging with dead phrases and simple-minded slogans. Yet this rhetorical car crash was widely commended, not least by Starmer himself, as showing his real strength as a political leader. Reform leader Nigel Farage’s pedestrian speeches – “You know what?” is his default phrase to underline what a frank and engaging fellow he is – won him an undeserved reputation for silver-tongued eloquence. 

Internet platforms are to blame for much but have put oratory back in business as an essential political tool. One of the attractive features of the US midterm elections was that listening to what was said at political rallies was often a pleasurable experience. 

Of course, this was still only true of a minority of candidates such as Senator Jon Ossoff in Georgia, James Talarico in Texas and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. But all can hold a live audience for hours and attract hundreds of thousands – and occasionally millions – of viewers online. The same is true of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who is also exceptionally adept in turning the most hostile questions to his advantage without appearing evasive or aggressive.

Trump always had the skills of a TV host, the most important of which is never to be boring whatever else you do. Mocked by the media for spewing out fake facts and crude abuse, his obsessive interest is with ratings – audience size – regardless of whether they like or dislike or believe him. 

Like a journalist, he knows what makes a headline, enabling him to get endless free exposure provided by TV companies that detest him. He and Vance long had an open goal, because nobody would listen to Kamala Harris or Joe Biden for fun.

Beneath the Radar

I was sorry to see that this week that Russian security forces finally closed down Novaya Gazeta, once the best independent newspaper in Russia. 

When I was a correspondent in Moscow between 1999 and 2002, they published occasional articles by me. To be a Russian journalist working for the paper was high up among the dangerous trades, with six or seven killed. I knew the most famous of them, Anna Politkovskaya, whom I first met in Chechnya during the war there when she was exposing Russian atrocities. I was unsurprised when she was shot dead on the stairs to her apartment in Moscow in 2006. It was fairly obvious that Russian security or their Chechen proxies were the culprits.

The paper, founded in 1993 though online since 2022, was perhaps the last active beneficiary of Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev’s glasnost policy still in business. Founded with money from Gorbachev’s Nobel Peace Prize, the Chechen wars made the paper internationally famous. But the Ukraine war, which it also opposed and criticised, finally killed the paper off. 

“There are different ways to commit murder,” said co-founder and former editor-in-chief Dmitry Muratov. “They chose to strangle us.”

Cockburn’s Picks

A crucial question in post-general election Israel is whether or not the opposition to Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, led by Gadi Eisenkot, can manoeuvre successfully – and without splitting their 48-seat bloc – to secure the backing of the two Arab Israeli parties in the Knesset. 

Joint List and Ra’am hold 19 of the 120 seats. The Arab Israeli parties say they are willing to back an anti-Netanyahu coalition, but the Eisenkot bloc is pledged not to form a government dependent on their support. 

I enjoyed this interview with former Israeli PM and ex-Israel Defence Forces (IDF) chief of staff Ehud Barak in which he argues that if Netanyahu was opposition leader, he would not have the slightest hesitation in doing such a deal. Israeli generals tend to achieve wisdom after they leave politics.

news.text: p>This week on NL Hafta, Abhinandan Sekhri, Manisha Pande, Anand Vardhan and Raman Kirpal discuss India’s latest poverty estimates and the US midterm elections. They are joined by Nitin Bharti, assistant professor at the University of Western Australia and South and Southeast Asia coordinator at the World Inequality Lab, and Joyojeet Pal, professor at the University of Michigan’s School of Information, whose research focuses on technology, democracy and politics.The discussion begins with the World Bank’s latest Poverty and Equity Brief, which says India's extreme poverty declined from 27.1 percent to 2.6 percent between 2011 and 2023.Nitin explains, “If the consumption of one person per day is about, let's say, 106 rupees or so, and if you consume more than that, you are above the moderate poverty line.” That works out to around Rs 3,200 a month, while the extreme poverty threshold is only around Rs 2,200.He also points to the 233 million people who remain below the Rs 3,000-a-month threshold.“The headline figure should have been that, yes, there has been some achievement, but you still have 233 million people who are consuming less than Rs 3,000 a month,” says Nitin.Raman Kirpal brings the conversation to the political use of poverty and welfare. Recalling an old Ministry of Finance study, he says one person had benefited from 27 different poverty-alleviation schemes and was still poor. “Poverty has served as a political tool also,” Raman says. “Politicians use it very often.”The second half of the episode turns to the midterm elections in the United States, where Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress. Joyojeet joins the panel to discuss what the result means for Donald Trump, MAGA and the wider American right.Joyojeet sees the result as a major setback for Trump’s movement, but not for conservatism itself. “This could be the end of the MAGA movement,” he says. “Absolutely not the end of the conservative movement.”He points to the cost of living as one of the issues that hurt Trump with his own base, arguing that voters increasingly felt the impact of his policies in their everyday lives.“The price of gas is clearly one that hurts his MAGA base,” Joyojeet says.The discussion also looks at the growing backlash against Big Tech, data centres and corporate influence in American politics. Joyojeet argues that voters are increasingly uncomfortable with the power technology companies exercise over their lives. “People have realised there’s ways in which tech is kind of taking over their lives,” he says.He points to Abdul El-Sayed’s Senate campaign in Michigan, which made AI regulation a central political issue. Joyojeet says El-Sayed was unusual among politicians in treating AI as a defining political question rather than simply another technology story.“AI is the main issue going ahead,” Joyojeet recalls him arguing, alongside a call for much stronger government regulation of the technology.All this and more..Hafta letters: Political unrest, AI anxiety and an app that needs an updateIf you want to write to Hafta, click here. news.title: 'Defeated Goliath': Did faith help Democrats flip key midterm races?
news.text:
As Democrat James Talarico of Texas delivered his acceptance speech Tuesday in Austin after his decisive U.S. Senate race win over Republican Ken Paxton, a large placard in front of him featured the words, “Love Thy Neighbor.”

That message seemed to resonate with voters nationwide, who vastly backed Democrats in a sweeping series of victories that some saw as a humanitarian rejection of federal policies such as overly aggressive immigration enforcement, unauthorized war, efforts to stamp out diversity and economic measures that have left many families struggling.

Religion proved pivotal at the ballot box nationwide, experts say, shaping voter views on key issues that turned previously red states blue. Faith was also brandished by candidates like Talarico to appeal to the electorate, even as conservatives blasted his progressive Christianity; in some cases, religion was weaponized by opponents, as in Islamophobic attacks and ad campaigns in Michigan and Texas.

“You did see some rejection of Republicans, especially with Hispanic Catholics in Texas,” said Michael Moreland, director of the Eleanor H. McCullen Center for Law, Religion and Public Policy at Villanova University in Pennsylvania. “Especially along the South Texas border, aspects of the administration’s immigration enforcement alienated a lot of voters. President Trump in 2024 peeled off a lot of those voters, but he lost them Tuesday night.”

Democrat megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton flipped a U.S. Senate seat in Kansas, while in Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton was elected both the state’s first Jewish and female governor, her Judaism informing her progressive platform.

Meanwhile, a record seven Muslims were elected to Congress nationwide, including Democrat physician Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who became the nation’s first Muslim U.S. senator. The number could rise to eight, depending on how California Democrat Aisha Wahab fares in her race for the state’s 14th Congressional district seat.

Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian and grandson of a Baptist preacher, was among several candidates who charted rare territory for white Democrats by making religion a central part of his campaign, citing scripture and stressing his Biblical grounding.

Dubbed “Talafreako” by President Donald Trump, Talarico kicked off his acceptance speech by using the Bible story of David and Goliath as a metaphor for his race against Paxton and “billionaire megadonors” like Elon Musk, who spent nearly $230 million to support Paxton’s campaign against Talarico.

“We went up against our own Goliath – the richest man in the world, the most powerful man in the world and the entire D.C. establishment,” Talarico said. Comparing himself to the shepherd boy who wielded a slingshot to slay his mightier foe, he told the crowd: “You were my slingshot. The people of Texas were my slingshot. And tonight, we defeated Goliath.”

Swing to Dems more pronounced among some faiths

Nationwide, exit polls conducted by NBC News revealed sizable shifts among several groups in the midterms compared to the 2024 election. Just under half of Catholics backed Republican candidates in the midterms, NBC found, compared to 59% who voted for Trump in 2024.

Jewish voters, meanwhile, swung the other way, NBC found: While 78% supported Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris in 2024, 68% voted for Democrats in this year’s midterms.

"Donald Trump said voters should pretend he was on the ballot in the midterms, and Jewish Americans did just that," Halie Soifer, CEO of the Jewish Democratic Council of America, said in a statement. "Jewish voters are not a monolith, but they widely disapprove of Donald Trump. This, coupled with the strength of the Democratic candidates who flipped red seats blue, led to overwhelming support for Democrats among Jewish voters in this election.”

Among religiously unaffiliated voters, NBC found, 27% supported Trump in 2024, compared to 20% who favored Republican candidates this fall.

Meanwhile, 86% of Muslims supported Democratic candidates in 2026 – the share wasn’t tallied in 2024 – while slightly fewer Protestants or other Christians supported Republican candidates this year compared with 2024.

Exit polls conducted by the Council on American-Islamic Relations indicated the Iran war, the economy, rising Islamophobia and Israel’s war in Gaza were foremost in their midterm voting choices. “Rising Islamophobia strengthened their motivation to vote,” the council said in a statement. “They overwhelmingly backed Democrats, but many remain unconvinced that either party listens to their concerns.”

During his race for Michigan’s Senate seat, El-Sayed was dismissed as a “jihadist” by Trump and accused of links to terrorist groups, both without evidence. Others criticized him for what they saw as a failure to sufficiently denounce antisemitism.

Frank Lacopo, an assistant professor of history at Southeast Missouri State University in Cape Girardeau, said such comments backfired with voters concerned with other issues.

“It really seems like El-Sayed’s more secular messaging on affordability was more effective,” Lacopo said. “What he showed people in Michigan was a vision of an American who happens to be Muslim.”

Did Catholics feel betrayed by Trump, GOP?

More than 50 million Catholics live in the U.S., with about 53% identifying as Republican, according to the Pew Research Center. Accounting for about a quarter of U.S. voters, they represent a broad political spectrum.

“It’s hard to neatly categorize the Catholic vote, because it depends on other factors – whether they’re white Catholics, Hispanic Catholics, young Catholics or more churchgoing ones,” Moreland said.

Kelsey Reinhardt, president and CEO of Catholic Vote, a conservative political advocacy organization based in Carmel, Indiana, said Catholics’ midterm swing toward Democrats reflected the broad concerns of the American electorate.

“In this election, Catholics are representative of the American population writ large,” Reinhardt said. “They care about necessities. The socioeconomic stratosphere of Catholics is pretty ordinary.”

In 2024, she said, Catholic voters largely believed Trump would be a greater arbiter of Catholic values. This time around, some may have felt betrayed by Trump’s broken anti-war promises, while anti-abortion advocates likely felt the president hasn’t done enough to advance their cause.

“The Catholic vote is soft Republican when there’s a Republican who advances their ideals,” Reinhardt said. “But they swing back when they feel their values are not being met. The Iran war was a factor too, but I’m not sure whether it’s an issue because it was declared immoral by the pope or because people didn’t want a forever war.”

Catholic concerns loomed large at the state level, such as in Virginia, where local bishops led a furious campaign that unsuccessfully sought to mobilize voters to reject ballot measures expanding abortion rights and removing wordage in the state constitution strictly defining marriage as between a man and woman.

“That was one where Catholics were heroic in their efforts,” Reinhardt said. “But 700,000 Catholics in Virginia won’t overturn the majority there.”

Lacopo thinks a factor that may have been a factor in Catholics’ Democratic swing is the Catholic church’s growing presence online.

“It’s important not to underestimate the power that Catholic church messaging on social media has on Catholics,” he said. “Even if they’re not practicing Catholics. A lot of Americans began to subscribe to Vatican News when Leo became pope, and they identify with him as an American.”

Pope Leo XIV’s fluency in both English and Spanish allows him to reach a wide swath of voters, he said. Meanwhile, the pope’s social media features a constant feed of direct quotes from the Chicago-born pontiff that help American followers see him as someone representing “a more accepting, open-arms version of Christianity.”

In general, Lacopo feels Democrats fielded better quality candidates who appealed to voters, with faith part of the package in states like Texas and Kansas.

“Talarico was absolutely perfect as a candidate for Texas because he had a way of speaking that came from his background of training as a Presbyterian minister,” Lacopo said. “He was able to use Christian messaging in a way that couldn’t be countered by Republicans.”

He noted Talarico’s acceptance speech also focused on what many consider the central tenets of Christian teaching, the notion of loving God and one’s neighbor – a message he thinks resonated not just with Texas Latinos anxious over immigration policy but with the kind of voters who plant signs reading “No Human Being is Illegal” in their front yards.

“I’m surprised and not surprised at the same time that Democrats have taken so long to latch on to that,” Lacopo said. “Even if you’re a secular voter and don’t practice religion, you can relate to the second part of that message.”

news.title: Reporting the ideas at the center of our political moment
news.text:
As I write this, the Monitor’s national news desk is scrambling to cover the aftermath of the Democratic wave in the U.S. midterm elections. Our reporters have crisscrossed the country – from Michigan to Texas, California to Maine – to talk with voters, policymakers, and candidates. Our goal is to not simply document the winners and losers, but to try to better understand the big ideas shaping the country, and to find those glimmers of compromise and shared values that might lay the foundation for civil and effective governance.

Our latest in political reporting is on our website – please take a look.

In this issue, we delve into a subject that was at the core of this recent election – and has, according to much research, undermined the confidence of many Americans in their government.

In May of this year, Politico and Public First found that 80% of 2024 Kamala Harris voters and 77% of Donald Trump voters agreed with the statement: “There is too much money in American politics.”

A YouGov poll from last year found that 76% of Americans (84 % of Democrats, 68% of Republicans, and 77% of independents) agreed that the “appearance of wealthy donors or corporations gaining influence over or access to elected officials causes me to lose faith in this democracy.”

I first reached out to Jeffrey Winters, a political science professor at Northwestern University, after I heard him talk about his recent book, “The Blind Spot: How Oligarchs Dominate Our Democracy.”

I was struck by his argument that oligarchy is structurally baked into our political system. But I was even more taken by his lack of partisanship, and the calm, historically minded, and above-the-fray approach he took to an issue that is riling both sides of the political aisle. I found myself thinking of his work repeatedly as I read about the midterms – including our reporting about artificial intelligence companies pouring funds into both Democratic and Republican campaigns.

(Dr. Winters urged me not to call these funds “donations.” They are, he told me, “political investments.”)

You can read his piece on page 25. It is the second installment of our new “terms” essays – writings by scholars and thinkers on common words that have a rich history and nuance worthy of exploration.

If you missed Harry Boyte and Trygve Throntveit’s essay, “Reclaiming citizenship,” which ran in the Nov. 2 issue, check it out on our website. You’ll find it under “What does citizenship mean? A case for a broader definition.” And if you have suggestions for a term that you think deserves a deep dive, please get in touch.
news.summary: Our reporting delves into the ideas underlying our political moment. In this issue of the magazine, we explore the concept of American oligarchy.

news.title: Democrats Won By Rebuking President Trump – And Embracing Their Hotness
news.text:
Democrats won back the House and the Senate by rebuking President Donald Trump — and they looked damn good doing so.

The 2026 midterms were hornier than ever as many Democrats and their online campaigns leaned into the fact that the candidates were easy on the eyes. 

Michigan Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed wore tight-fitting black shirts and showed off his biceps while bench-pressing and challenging Vice President JD Vance to the weight room.

The official TikTok for the Democratic Party released a video captioned “Phone on DND [do not disturb] I told my boyfriend that I’m busy” for Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff that involved multiple close-ups of the incumbent and his visible forearms set to Saucy Santana’s rap.

Meanwhile, Montana Rep.-elect Sam Forstag wore an unbuttoned shirt during a CNN interview and used a chainsaw for a campaign ad.

The new class of politicians is not like the buttoned-up Democrats of the past. Lauren Kapp, a digital strategist who helped with Kamala Harris’s 2024 campaign and launched the Democratic Party’s first TikTok account, said the type of fancam edits of candidates being released now “would have never made it through approvals back then.”

Now, “Democrats at large and the DNC [Democratic National Committee] are starting to understand the attention economy in which we live,” Kapp said. “In order to break through, you have to do or say something worth paying attention to within the first couple of frames of a video ― not seconds.” 

And one of the quickest ways to get a voter’s attention online is to start showing off a candidate’s physical attributes. For some voters, “they’re not going to read a New York Times story, but they’ll watch that TikTok of Abdul El-Sayed lifting with Hasan Piker,” said Monica Venzke, a Democratic communications professional.

She noted that using a candidate’s good looks is “such a good fundraising tool, and I think that definitely led to some of these victories.”

Venzke’s passion project, “Boyfriends We Deserve,” highlights the attractiveness of Democratic candidates on social media. Her account’s endorsement of Jack Schlossberg even got used in a fundraising text that read in part: “A good boyfriend is someone who listens. Same with a good Rep.”

Venzke said the “thirst trappification” of political candidates is not just meant to appeal to women and queer people who may be physically attracted to watching these candidates up close. She cited the success of Sam Forstag, who became the first Democrat elected to the House in Montana in more than 30 years. In the months before his race, Forstag leaned into his physical prowess and released a video of himself fixing a tire while discussing “how to fix a system rigged in favor of the ultrarich” like Elon Musk. 

“It kind of gives straight guys... permission to be a Democrat again,” Venzke said. “If this Montanan smoke jumper who fixes up trucks and jumps out of planes to put out fires can be a Democrat, so can I.”

The 2026 Midterms Were A Masculinity Contest. That’s Not New.

Perceived hotness is not a new bipartisan issue. Trump has long had a habit of calling out the physical attributes of his allies, most recently praising Jon Husted’s butt as a “pile of muscle” at a political rally for the midterms. 

“U.S. elections have always been masculinity contests ― which is one reason women are often at such a disadvantage in them ― and it’s just the ways that candidates perform masculinity that changes,” said Dan Cassino, a professor of government and politics at Fairleigh Dickinson University.

Before El-Sayed bench-pressed 315 pounds on social media, candidates would use their military experience, height or powerful voice to signal their masculinity, Cassino noted. 

“Even in the 18th century, people were making fun of John Adams for being ‘fat,’ and more than a hundred years ago, Teddy Roosevelt made physical fitness and activity a big part of his political appeal,” he cited. “One of George Washington’s qualifications was his height.”

But Washington wasn’t being remixed to Megan Thee Stallion’s “Big Ole Freak” by an official TikTok account for the Democratic Party. Cassino thinks the current array of thirsty campaign videos isn’t necessarily about sex appeal, but about establishing a candidate’s strength and perseverance, which are coded as masculine behaviors.

“It’s not great that Americans think masculine traits are synonymous with leadership traits, but as long as they do, both male and female candidates are going to be trying to prove that they have those masculine traits so that voters will trust them as leaders,” Cassino said. “The fact that muscles and appearance are hard to get, and require work, and can’t be easily faked makes them a really valuable signal.”

Of course, charming looks and an impressive physique may get a voter’s attention, but it takes something more to keep it.

“Once you have seen them, it is their job to win your money and your support,” Venzke said, noting that “obviously John Ossoff is gorgeous. I’m not a Georgian, but I would vote for him if he was ugly because he’s a great candidate.”

And for these midterms, showcasing good-looking candidates with clear anti-Trump policies was a winning Democratic strategy –– and a sharp counterpoint to the hypermasculine approach that Trump’s MAGA allies have taken. 

“After so much of the manosphere propaganda that is coming from the right, it’s nice to see the Democrats also showing they can win in this game and to use this to their own advantage,” said Einav Rabinovitch-Fox, a historian who writes about gender and politics. “It is good that the Democrats are presenting their own version of the ‘sexy’ candidate to run counter to the MAGA masculine men.”

The smoldering campaign videos may have ended for now, but that doesn’t mean the newly elected candidates’ hotness will be suppressed. Venzke expects the thirst-trap strategy to shift as these candidates go to Congress and speak up in Senate hearings: “These super sexy, manly guys, I’m going to see looking super hot in suits all day,” she said. 

Take it from the newly elected candidates. After his win, El-Sayed’s official TikTok account released a video of a black V-neck shirt getting replaced by a black suit. The caption reads: “Change is coming.”

news.title: Anthony Constantino’s Post-Election Crashout
news.text:
At an election eve rally in upstate New York, Republican congressional candidate Anthony Constantino told the crowd he had a dramatic announcement: Donald Trump was wrong about one thing. An audible gasp rippled through the converted airplane hangar. What could it possibly be? 

“Fake news” wasn’t accurate, Constantino said. “It’s actually evil news.” 

The candidate went on to gesture at the press pen and tell the crowd to take photos of its nefarious inhabitants. The campaign had not granted me credentials, so, like everyone else, I turned my attention to the people Constantino said “should be ashamed” of themselves. What Constantino did not seem to realize was that the most embarrassing thing about the event was that it was happening at all.

One day before the midterms, JD Vance and Donald Trump Jr. were flying into a district the president won by more than 20 points in 2024. Polls showed the race as a dead heat, despite Constantino loaning his campaign $17 million of the fortune he amassed through his novelty company Sticker Mule. Vance and Trump Jr., who arrived on Air Force Two accompanied by the soundtrack of Top Gun, were the reinforcements. 

So, too, was Carol Constantino, who introduced her 44-year-old son as a once challenging kid who nevertheless deserved Republicans’ support. “I’ll also admit that Anthony wasn’t easy,” Carol said about what he was like after her husband passed away when Anthony was a boy. “He was a challenge at times. He was stubborn.”

On Tuesday, Constantino won New York’s 21st congressional district, which runs from around Albany up to the Canadian border, by about 2 points. It was an abysmal showing considering that Rep. Elise Stefanik carried the district by 24 points in 2024. In typical fashion, Constantino showed no humility. Instead, he celebrated his victory with the venom that marked his campaign from start to finish. Come January, Constantino, who will be one of just two GOP freshmen from the Northeast in the new Congress, is in pole position to be the much diminished Republican caucus’ most uncontrollable loudmouth. 

As I wrote in a profile earlier this year, Constantino prevailed over the New York GOP establishment in his primary thanks to a Trump endorsement and millions of dollars of his money. He is one of the most unusual candidates I have ever covered. In addition to being a sticker mogul, Constantino has moonlighted as a rapper and stand-up comic. (Example: A bit about Kamala Harris supporters vomiting before and after he put his penis in their mouths.) He also spent much of the past decade living in Mexico pursuing a new career as a technically professional boxer. 

Stefanik is a Harvard graduate who in 2014 became the youngest woman ever elected to Congress. Despite attending Albany Academy at the same time, she and Constantino have radically different public images. As I’ve written : 

During his campaign launch held in front of a wall of free turkeys, Constantino labeled Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez a “perra falsa”—Spanish for fake bitch. He told Gerard Kassar, the head of New York’s Conservative Party, to get “his ass” in a boxing ring, so he could punch him “in the fucking face legally.” In the video for his Zohran Mamdani diss track—which includes the line “fuck you bitch” and includes a reference to the New York mayor’s “boy Osama”—he makes a throat-slitting gesture. In keeping with this thuggish persona, Constantino’s close associates have been accused or found guilty of kidnapping, stealing money from a youth baseball league, and lying to Congress. 

On election night, Constantino rambled for nearly 30 minutes, while wearing a Mike Amiri trucker hat that retails for nearly $400. He thanked his campaign adviser Roger Stone, who Constantino said had told him to be nicer during the campaign. (That may be a first for Stone, a convicted felon and infamous, self-proclaimed “dirty trickster.”) He then had his buddy Jason “Greatness” Jensen—a face-tattooed white man who plays an important role in the Constantino cinematic universe—do a brief rap: “He backed by God, plus he Trump-endorsed.” (God’s position in the race could not be verified.)

As the remarks continued, Constantino increasingly resembled the difficult boy his mom had mentioned raising at the previous day’s rally. He blamed the press for his failure to win by the 20-point margin he’d wanted. The reporters who covered him were “scumbags” and a “bunch of fucking assholes.” Even the members of the press who weren’t “bad people,” were “evil” for failing to expose their colleagues. Pointing to a reporter, he continued, “Look at that asshole, right there … Take a picture of him … [City & State reporter] Kate Lisa, another fucking asshole.”

From there, he had one of those reporters kicked out of the event. “He’s so angry right now, you can just see it in his eyes,” Constantino said in what came across as textbook projection. “He’s just a angry motherfucker,” the congressman elect later added. As a reminder, this was a victory speech. It is hard to imagine what a concession speech might have sounded like. By way of a closing message, he said that Trump should consider “freeing” Sean Combs, the hip-hop mogul known as “Diddy” who was convicted last year of transporting people across state lines for prostitution.

Constantino’s invective was not limited to the stage. Around 3:15 a.m. on election night, Constantino sent a text message to Schenectady County GOP Chair Liz Joy that stated, “Resign you scumbag.” (Joy shared the screenshot on X.) About 10 minutes later, the congressman elect posted on X that “NY-21 Republican Chairs are objectively a group of scammers,” adding that Bruce Blakeman, the defeated GOP nominee for New York governor, “was in on the con.” 

In a public reply on Thursday, Blakeman called Constantino “by far the worst candidate I ever encountered.” He is not alone in the assessment; the editorial board of the Albany Times Union wrote in June that it could not “recall ever meeting a more unsuitable candidate.” 

Constantino’s post-victory crashout continued into Friday, when he wrote that a female New York reporter is “33 and looks 53.” When an X user who goes by the name JohnsCow (follower count: 7) called Constantino “Low IQ,” Constantino replied at 2:02 a.m., “My IQ is 132.”

After the rally on Monday, I headed over to the press area to talk to a fellow member of the “evil news” whom I recognized from attacks posted on Constantino’s X feed. But our conversation was cut short by a surreal scene: Constantino was rolling past us on a mobility scooter with a white-bearded veteran more or less sitting on his lap. Moving silently across the floor of the old hangar, the candidate finally seemed to be having a good time.

He had just one question for his staff: “Where’s my mom?”

news.title: EXCLUSIVE: DC Workers Pay For Ridiculous Amount Of Porn On Job, GPS Data Suggests
news.text:
People in Washington, D.C., consume pornography on OnlyFans at high rates during the workday, according to Max Anderson, CEO of OnlyFinder, whose company published a report on OnlyFans spending.

People in the nation’s capital spend more on OnlyFans content per capita than any of the 50 states in the US, according to the OnlyFinder’s OnlyFans Wrapped 2026 report. OnlyFans spending in the District drops off heavily at night, suggesting commuters consume a disproportionate amount of pornographic content during the workday, Anderson told the Daily Caller News Foundation. 

While the public report does not present data related to the time spent on OnlyFans, Anderson explained the firm’s internal finding about pornography spending in the District to the DCNF. 

“People who work in D.C. are heavily using OnlyFans inside the boundaries of the District of Columbia during the workday, and then their usage drops off a cliff when they go home to the suburbs at night,” Anderson told the DCNF. 

“The data certainly supports that D.C. workers are heavily using OnlyFans during the workday,” Anderson told the DCNF.

OnlyFinder is an online service that works as a search engine and discovery tool for OnlyFans content. OnlyFans does not have a curated homepage or search feature embedded on the website, so most internet traffic searching for OnlyFans content is routed through OnlyFinder, according to Anderson. OnlyFinder began reporting the estimated spending on OnlyFans content in 2025. 

The population of D.C. spends $277,248.85 per 10,000 adults on OnlyFans content, OnlyFinder report estimates by tracking the geographic location of devices engaging with the site’s content. 

Around 23% of D.C. jobs are in the federal government, and federal workers have previously come under fire for watching porn on the job in a 2017 investigation from NBC News 4. The investigation alleged that over 100 federal workers were sifting through pornography for up to six hours a day on their office computers.

OnlyFans is a UK-based subscription service platform used almost exclusively for pornography and not-safe-for-work content. Subscribers pay a monthly fee to access content from producers, but per Anderson, a significant portion of subscriber spending is on pay-per-view personalized content and direct messaging. (RELATED: Chinese-Linked Network Of More Than 400 AI Apps Hid Deepfake Porn Tools From Apple, Google)

The United States is the largest market for OnlyFans, with Americans spending $4.9 billion on the platform in 2026, per the OnlyFinder report. People in the Portland, Oregon, greater metropolitan area spent $459,994.20 per 10,000 adults on OnlyFans, more than any other metro area in the world. 

States that voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election spent about 13% more on OnlyFans per capita than states that President Donald Trump won. The top 12 states for per capita OnlyFans spending were all Democrat-led states. 

Over 90% of OnlyFans spenders are men, Anderson said. Men report feeling lonelier than ever, and 90% of men consume pornography at least once a month, according to a study published by the National Institutes of Health.
